## DAILY INTELLIGENCE BRIEF

### 1. Russia and Ukraine exchange major long-range attacks
Ukraine launched one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, with Russia claiming 822 drones intercepted nationwide and around 600 directed toward Moscow. At least six people were reported killed in Russia. Russia simultaneously struck Kyiv, Kryvyi Rih, Kremenchuk and other Ukrainian locations with missiles and 106 drones; Ukrainian regional authorities reported at least seven civilians killed and 51 injured.

**Why it matters:** Both sides are expanding attacks far beyond the front, targeting industrial, logistics and energy infrastructure while increasing risks to civilians and economic activity.

### 2. NATO aircraft downs drone over Romania
A Spanish F-18 operating under NATO air-policing arrangements shot down a drone that entered Romanian airspace from Moldova near Galati. Romanian officials did not identify its origin, although a NATO spokesperson said it appeared to be Russian.

**Why it matters:** The incident highlights the growing risk that the Ukraine war could spill into NATO territory. It also demonstrates a more active allied response to repeated airspace violations along NATO’s eastern flank.

### 3. Ukraine targets Russian missile and logistics infrastructure
Ukraine said it struck a Russian Bastion coastal missile system in occupied Crimea, including launch positions used for Onyx and Zircon missiles. Kyiv also reported attacks on a missile-propellant facility in Russia’s Rostov region, a military railway bridge in occupied Zaporizhzhia and ammunition and logistics sites in Donetsk. Damage claims remain independently unverified.

**Why it matters:** The attacks indicate a coordinated effort to degrade Russia’s ability to conduct missile strikes and sustain forces in occupied southern Ukraine.

### 4. Intelligence points to possible expansion of North Korean support for Russia
Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect North Korea may send an additional 30,000–50,000 troops to Russia, potentially freeing Russian units for frontline operations. Ukrainian intelligence also says Pyongyang has supplied 148 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles since 2025 and may deploy a missile unit to Russia’s Voronezh region. No concrete evidence of the reported new troop deployment was presented.

**Why it matters:** A larger North Korean role could strengthen Russia’s manpower and missile capacity while giving Pyongyang additional combat and weapons experience with implications for Asia-Pacific security.

### 5. Middle East ceasefire tracks remain under pressure
Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed at least 11 people; Israel said two Hezbollah commanders were targeted. Separately, a Hamas delegation arrived in Cairo for talks on advancing a Gaza ceasefire roadmap, while Israel has rejected elements requiring withdrawal from territory it controls.

**Why it matters:** The Lebanon strikes test the Israel-Hezbollah truce, while major disagreements over withdrawal and Hamas’s disarmament continue to obstruct progress in Gaza.

## WATCH

- **Romania drone investigation:** Confirmation of the drone’s origin and whether NATO adjusts air-policing or engagement procedures.
- **North Korean deployment:** Evidence that additional troops or a ballistic-missile unit are moving into Russia.
- **Strategic-strike damage:** Independent assessment of the Bastion system, Rostov missile-propellant facility and other Russian logistics targets hit by Ukraine.

## North Korea–Russia Military Cooperation Deepens

Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect North Korea may deploy an additional 30,000–50,000 troops to Russia, after an estimated 14,000–15,000 were sent from late 2024. Ukrainian intelligence also says Pyongyang has supplied KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles and may deploy a missile unit to Russia’s Voronezh region. Kim Jong Un and Vladimir Putin separately reaffirmed broad bilateral cooperation.

**Why it matters:** A larger North Korean deployment could free Russian forces for operations in Ukraine and give Pyongyang valuable combat experience. Expanded missile and military cooperation could also strengthen North Korea’s capabilities and affect security calculations on the Korean Peninsula and across the Asia-Pacific.

## Iran War Strains Gulf–US Security Relations

Gulf governments are reportedly increasingly frustrated with Washington’s handling of the conflict with Iran and the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a new defense agreement, described as an effort to diversify regional security partnerships. Meanwhile, Iran has not agreed to resume formal negotiations with the United States, although intermediaries including Pakistan, Qatar and Oman remain active.

**Why it matters:** Prolonged disruption in the Strait of Hormuz threatens global energy supplies, trade routes and prices. Gulf efforts to broaden their defense relationships could gradually alter the region’s longstanding dependence on US security guarantees, although Gulf states still rely heavily on American weapons and intelligence.

## Sustained Chinese Military Pressure Around Taiwan

Taiwan tracked 11 Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels and two official ships in a 24-hour period. Seven aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line, prompting Taiwan to deploy aircraft, ships and coastal missile systems. The activity came amid renewed expressions of US congressional support for Taiwan and discussions on defense spending and drone cooperation.

**Why it matters:** Repeated Chinese operations around Taiwan normalize a higher level of military pressure and increase the risk of miscalculation. Closer US–Taiwan defense cooperation, particularly involving drones and resilient supply chains, is likely to remain a source of friction between Washington and Beijing.

## WATCH

- **Korean Peninsula tensions:** South Korea fired warning shots after North Korean troops crossed the military demarcation line. Upcoming US–South Korean exercises could prompt further North Korean military responses despite Seoul’s call for renewed dialogue.
- **Japan’s wartime remembrance:** Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Yasukuni Shrine offering and omission of remorse from her memorial address could generate diplomatic criticism from neighboring countries and intensify scrutiny of Japan’s defense expansion.

## 1. Ukraine Mounts Major Long-Range Drone Assault

Ukraine launched one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, with Russia claiming it intercepted 822 drones nationwide, including about 200 over the Moscow region. Russian officials reported at least six deaths in the Moscow and Rostov regions, alongside damage to homes, transport infrastructure and major logistics facilities. Ukraine also said it struck a missile-fuel plant in Rostov. Russia simultaneously attacked Kyiv, Kryvyi Rih, Sumy and other Ukrainian locations with missiles and drones, killing at least five people, according to Ukrainian officials.

**Why it matters:** The scale of the attacks demonstrates Ukraine’s expanding ability to threaten targets deep inside Russia, disrupt aviation and impose economic costs. Continued Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities and industrial sites show that both sides are intensifying long-range operations.

## 2. NATO Jet Downs Drone Over Romania

A Spanish F-18 conducting NATO air-policing duties shot down a drone after it entered Romanian airspace. NATO said the drone appeared to be Russian, while Romania said it had entered from Moldova; the incident remains under investigation.

**Why it matters:** The interception represents a direct NATO military response to an airborne incursion linked to the war. Repeated drone breaches increase the risk of escalation or accidental confrontation between Russia and the alliance.

## 3. Ukraine Claims Strike on Russian Bastion System in Crimea

The Ukrainian Navy said it struck the launch positions and deployment site of a Russian Bastion coastal missile system in occupied Crimea, causing significant equipment and personnel losses. Ukraine also reported attacks on a railway bridge in occupied Zaporizhzhia and logistics and ammunition facilities in Donetsk. The damage has not been independently confirmed.

**Why it matters:** Bastion systems can launch Onyx and Zircon missiles against Ukrainian targets and are relatively scarce and costly. Damaging the system and associated logistics would support Ukraine’s broader effort to reduce Crimea’s value as a Russian missile, naval and supply hub.

## WATCH

- **Russian jet-powered drones:** Russia showcased the BM-35 attack drone, claiming a 200-kilometre range, high speed and resistance to electronic warfare. Its operational performance and production scale remain unclear.
- **European defence integration:** Poland’s foreign minister proposed a permanent “European Legion,” potentially including Ukrainian veterans after the war. Monitor whether the concept gains support from other European governments.
regional_summaries.middle_east:
## 1. US-Iran confrontation intensifies around Strait of Hormuz

Iran and the United States exchanged threats ahead of a reported deadline under the June Islamabad agreement for reaching an understanding on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said discussions with Oman were continuing but linked reopening to US acceptance of its conditions. Meanwhile, the US Central Command chief visited the USS *Abraham Lincoln*, which is supporting US operations against Iran and the blockade of Iranian ports.

**Why it matters:** The strait is a critical route for international energy shipments. Continued closure, military operations or miscalculation could disrupt trade and trigger broader regional escalation.

## 2. Israeli strikes test Lebanon ceasefire

Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed at least 11 people. Israel said the attacks killed two Hezbollah commanders, including a senior commander in the Badr regional division and a commander from the elite Radwan Force. Israel described one strike as retaliation for a Hezbollah drone attack that wounded three soldiers. Lebanon condemned the strikes, which were reported as the deadliest since the June truce.

**Why it matters:** The attacks and counterclaims of ceasefire violations increase the risk that the Israel-Hezbollah front will return to sustained conflict despite US-mediated efforts to preserve the truce.

## 3. Houthi attacks close Mocha port and widen Yemen escalation

Yemen’s Mocha port suspended operations after more than 25 Houthi missile attacks in recent days. Port officials reported seven deaths and approximately $16 million in losses. Government-aligned authorities also reported missile and drone attacks on residential areas in Marib, injuring four people. The Houthis said their Mocha attacks targeted military assets belonging to Saudi-backed forces.

**Why it matters:** Renewed attacks threaten to unravel the relative lull in Yemen’s war. Mocha’s proximity to the Bab al-Mandab shipping chokepoint also raises risks for Red Sea maritime security and commercial traffic.

## WATCH

- **Hormuz negotiations:** Monitor the deadline under the Islamabad agreement, Oman-mediated contacts and any change in US or Iranian military activity around the strait.
- **Lebanon ceasefire:** Further Israeli strikes or Hezbollah retaliation could indicate a shift from limited exchanges toward renewed large-scale fighting.

articles.title: Russia Unveils Jet-Powered BM-35 Drone With 217 Mph Speed
articles.body:
Russian propagandists have aired a segment showcasing the use of a jet-powered BM-35 attack drone, which they claim can reach speeds exceeding 350 km/h (217 mph) and cover distances up to 200 km (124 miles).
Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to President Volodymyr Zelensky, highlighted the report regarding the drone’s capabilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Russian operators featured in the segment, the BM-35 does not require complex preparation. They stated the drone can be launched within minutes from any terrain using a mobile platform.
The propagandists claimed that an operator can control the drone throughout its entire flight trajectory, essentially in a First-Person View (FPV) mode. They further asserted that Ukrainian electronic warfare (EW) systems do not affect the drone’s signal.
The BM-35 reportedly carries a 22-pounds warhead. The operators claimed the 124-mile range allows them to strike targets deep in the rear, while the speed of over 217 mph prevents Ukrainian interceptors from catching the apparatus.
According to the report, the components are prepared in advance at a warehouse, leaving only the assembly of the drone, installation of the warhead, and the launch to be completed at the firing position.
The operators stated that up to three drones can be launched simultaneously and that the warhead disperses up to a thousand fragmentation elements over a 650-feet (198-meter) radius upon detonation.
Drone Attacks Spark Large Fires at Wildberries Hubs Near Moscow
Foreign components in Russian weapons
The development follows recent reports from Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) regarding the integration of advanced foreign technology into new Russian weapons systems.
On Aug. 12, HUR reported that its specialists had identified an Nvidia Jetson Orin computer module inside Russia’s new S-71 Monochrome air-launched cruise missile.
The agency stated that the use of this module potentially indicates the integration of artificial intelligence technologies into the weapon.
The finding was published on the HUR’s War&Sanctions portal, which documents foreign electronic components found in Russian weapons. The intelligence agency noted that the latest research identified 35 foreign electronic components in the S-71 Monochrome.
Ukrainian specialists have also identified parts of a passive radar seeker that Russia has begun installing on Geran-2 drones, designed to detect and strike Ukrainian air-defense systems.
Additionally, researchers identified a Chinese Honpho TS130C-01 camera from a Geran-4 jet-powered drone and components of the active radar seeker used in Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile.
HUR stated that the continued discovery of foreign high-tech components demonstrates that Russia has been unable to fully replace them with domestic alternatives, underscoring the need for increased sanctions pressure.
The agency noted that limited production capacity prevents Russian forces from maintaining continuous, high-intensity drone launches, forcing them to build up reserves prior to major attacks.

articles.title: Ukraine launches one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, killing at least 6 people in Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine launches one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, killing at least 6 people in Russia
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones across Russia Sunday, killing at least six people in one of Kyiv’s largest aerial attacks of the war.
Kyiv has stepped up its attacks on Russia this year, with long-range missiles and swarms of drones increasingly targeting military industries and energy facilities. It has also increasingly pummeled giant Wildberries depots, burning billions of dollars’ worth of merchandise belonging to the Russian online retail giant and bringing the war home to the Russian public nearly 4½ years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that it had destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones overnight. Some 600 drones were detected headed toward the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, with a third of those destroyed over the Moscow region itself.
An 83-year-old man was killed after a Ukrainian drone hit a private home in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said. He also confirmed that a Ukrainian attack had sparked a blaze at a Wildberries warehouse in the town of Podolsk.
A drone attack targeted three towns in Russia’s southwestern Rostov region, killing five people, local Gov. Yury Slyusar said. The attack, with more than 150 drones, damaged several homes and a railway station and sparked a forest fire.
Russian strikes kill 5 in Ukraine
A Russian missile attack on Ukraine’s Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 14 others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media Sunday. He also said that one more person had been killed in the city of Sumy.
Elsewhere, a man and a woman both died when their home was hit by a Russian strike in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region, said Ivan Fedorov, the head of the local military administration.
More attacks sparked fires throughout the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, wounding six people.
“Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said. “Since this morning, air raid alerts have continued in many regions — the Russians launched another wave of drones.”
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Sunday that it had targeted a metallurgical plant in Kryvyi Rih and several military-industrial sites in Kyiv, including a manufacturing facility for Ukraine’s Flamingo missiles.
The domestically produced missiles are increasingly key to Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russia, with Zelenskyy announcing Saturday that Kyiv had used the weapons to attack a rocket research and production center in Samara approximately 900 kilometers (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
NATO jet downs drone in Romanian airspace
Romania’s Ministry of National Defense said Sunday that a Spanish Air and Space Force F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone that had entered Romanian airspace.
The drone’s entry into the NATO member’s airspace was detected by surveillance systems at 4:44 a.m., the ministry said, about 24 kilometers (14.9 miles) north of the eastern city of Galati near the border with neighboring Moldova. Moldova is a landlocked country between Ukraine and Romania.
A Spanish F-18 aircraft that was performing air policing duties “made radar contact with the target and received engagement approval,” the ministry said. “The drone was safely shot down by the F-18 aircraft at 05:01.”
Officials did not specify the drone’s origin.
The incident comes weeks after Romanian pilots shot down the three drones over three days from F-16 fighter jets, as Russia intensified attacks against Ukraine near the border. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Romania has reported dozens of drone incidents, including some that have crashed and exploded on its territory.
Acting Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said in a post on X that the Spanish deployment in Romania was scaled up “at the request of Romania and NATO to bolster the Eastern Flank following prior drone incidents,” and that it was Spain’s fourth such deployment.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

articles.title: World Insights: War shrine tributes on surrender day reveal Japan's lingering militarist obsession
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- Aug. 15 marks the 81st anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II. On the day, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sent a ritual offering to the notorious war-linked Yasukuni Shrine, while making no mention of "remorse" in her first war memorial address.
Analysts believe Japan's ruling authorities are persistently pushing to accelerate military expansion and rearmament and promoting right-wing historical views and narratives of "regional threats," with increasingly evident characteristics of "neo-militarism." They warn that today's Japan bears a striking resemblance to the Japan that embarked on a path of aggressive war in the past; if left unchecked, this trajectory poses a serious threat to regional peace and stability, and the international community should remain highly vigilant.
NO SIGN OF REMORSE
On Saturday, Takaichi made a "tamagushi" ritual offering to the Yasukuni Shrine, a symbol of the country's militarism and wartime aggression, in her capacity as president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Before attending the National Memorial Service for the War Dead, she turned toward the shrine across the road and bowed twice, clapped twice and bowed once from the parking area of Nippon Budokan hall, in an apparent act of Shinto worship.
Meanwhile, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and several other cabinet ministers showed up at the shrine earlier Saturday, marking the seventh consecutive year that sitting Japanese ministers have paid respects there on Aug. 15. LDP Secretary-General Shunichi Suzuki, other top ruling party executives, and a nonpartisan group of dozens of lawmakers also visited the shrine.
In her speech at the annual memorial held in Tokyo, Takaichi neither mentioned Japan's wars of aggression against its Asian neighbors nor expressed remorse or apology for the suffering they caused. She even altered a phrase traditionally used by previous prime ministers, changing "must never repeat the horrors of war" into "The horrors of war must never be repeated." Japanese media pointed out that the revised wording deliberately obscures the subject responsible for the war, thereby avoiding reflection on Japan's wartime aggression.
This is not the first time Takaichi has employed such rhetorical ambiguity. In speeches earlier this month at ceremonies commemorating the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, she merely stated that Japan "is adhering to the Three Non-Nuclear Principles," while remaining vague about whether her government would continue to uphold them. Some Japanese media criticized the ambiguity as evidence that the prime minister has failed to genuinely learn from history.
Takaichi has long been associated with controversial positions on historical issues. In 1994, she publicly questioned the Murayama government's apology and remorse over Japan's wartime aggression, arguing that a prime minister could not apologize on behalf of the Japanese people. In a television program in 2002, she described Japan's wartime actions as a "war for self-preservation and self-defense," drawing sharp criticism. She has also published articles on her official website endorsing the right-wing "Greater East Asia War" historical narrative and promoting the prewar Imperial Rescript on Education, a document widely associated with militarist ideology.
Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, said the ruling authorities not only lack reflection on Japan's aggression but also display a wartime logic disturbingly similar to that of the political leaders who led Japan into war more than 80 years ago.
Anatoly Koshkin, executive council member of the Russian Association of World War II Historians, said the ideological poison of militarism continues to spread in Japanese society; influenced by right-wing propaganda, many in the younger generation, who have no firsthand memories of the horrors of war, hope to see Japan's return as a major military power.
RAPID REMILITARIZATION
The Japanese government has long sought to bolster the country's military capabilities, gradually chipping away at the military constraints imposed by the postwar pacifist constitution and steadily hollowing out the long-standing principle of "exclusively defense-oriented policy."
Since Takaichi took office, her government has only hit the accelerator on military buildup.
At the institutional level, the Takaichi administration has been taking a series of aggressive moves, from seeking to revise the Three Non-Nuclear Principles when updating the country's three key security documents by the end of this year, to speeding up efforts to amend the pacifist constitution, aiming to make headway on a constitutional amendment proposal before next year's Liberal Democratic Party convention.
Meanwhile, a reform to centralize the country's intelligence apparatus is underway, including the establishment of a national intelligence agency, to tighten control over public opinion and facilitate military expansion.
In terms of military deployment and operations, the Takaichi administration has put offensive weapons into actual service, deploying long-range missiles with so-called "enemy base strike capabilities" in Japan for the first time and conducting the first test-firing of U.S.-made Tomahawk cruise missiles.
It has also accelerated efforts to expand the Self-Defense Forces' overseas presence, sending a large contingent of combat personnel to the Philippines for joint military drills for the first time, and is vigorously developing "new ways of warfare" and working to enhance sustained combat capabilities.
On the fiscal front, the Japanese government has significantly increased defense spending. A supplementary budget for fiscal 2025 allowed Japan to hit its target of raising defense-related spending to 2 percent of gross domestic product two years ahead of schedule, and the surge has continued unabated. With the initial defense budget for fiscal 2026 having reached a new record high, the defense budget request for fiscal 2027 is reportedly set to climb even further.
Economically, the Japanese authorities are trying to turn the defense industry into a new pillar for reviving the country's economy. In April this year, the Takaichi government revised the "three principles on transfer of defense equipment and technology" and their implementation guidelines, allowing the export of lethal weapons in principle, and thereby opening up markets for Japan's military industry.
Meanwhile, the country's 2026 defense white paper significantly expanded discussion of reinforcing defense production and technological bases, touting the defense business as a contributor to "Japan's economic growth."
In manipulating public opinion and perceptions, the Takaichi administration has not only continued to downplay, deny, and whitewash the history of Japanese aggression, but has also hyped up alleged "security threats" from neighboring countries, particularly the so-called "China threat," to pave the way for military expansion.
Takaichi has publicly claimed that a "Taiwan contingency" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" that could allow Japan to exercise the right of collective self-defense, and has cast China as "an unprecedented and the greatest strategic challenge."
Australian business strategy consultant Antony Hing said Japan is "very rapidly" shifting away from its pacifist constitution, and it could be in breach of its international legal obligations in acting the way it's acting.
Ling Tek Soon, senior lecturer at the Institute of China Studies of the University of Malaya, said that Japan is constantly pushing beyond the institutional boundaries of the postwar order, departing from the "peaceful nation" identity and development path it has long professed.
HISTORY'S WARNING
Japanese historians, including Masahiro Yamazaki, have pointed out that Japan's current political, military, economic and ideological trajectory bears striking similarities to the path the country took prior to World War II.
Following the Meiji Restoration, Japan gradually embarked on a course of militarist expansion abroad. During the 1930s, it responded to economic crisis with military buildup and external aggression. Military leaders, politicians and powerful business interests formed close alliances to stoke fears of "external threats" and "existential crisis" to mobilize public support for war. National resources were concentrated in the military sector, benefiting the military establishment and large industrial conglomerates while ordinary people bore the economic burden and ultimately became victims of war.
Today, a similar scenario is playing out again. Faced with domestic challenges such as prolonged economic stagnation, Japan's right-wing conservative forces view "breaking free from the post-war order" and becoming a "normal country" as a supposed way out.
Government resources continue to shift toward defense, with military expansion presented as a means of stimulating economic growth. At the same time, narratives emphasizing "external threats," denying historical aggression and reviving prewar militarist ideology are increasingly used for political and social mobilization, leading to a resurgence of militarism in Japan.
These trends have sparked strong protests and heightened vigilance among the Japanese public.
Yamazaki warned that the government's persistent emphasis on "external threats" could easily steer Japan into war once again. Akira Yamada, professor at Meiji University, said Japan's continued military buildup risks fueling a regional arms race that could become increasingly difficult to reverse once established.
Critics also argue that Japan's remilitarization carries growing domestic costs. As defense spending reaches record levels, military contractors have reaped substantial profits while social welfare and other livelihood-related expenditures face mounting pressure. The result, they say, is worsening public finances and increasing hardship for ordinary citizens.
Atsushi Koketsu, professor emeritus at Yamaguchi University, argued that the government's push for remilitarization comes at the expense of public welfare. "It is fundamentally wrong to place people's livelihoods in insecurity in exchange for so-called national security," he said.
Kim Joo-Yong, professor of history and culture at South Korea's Wonkwang University, said the truly responsible path for Japan is to confront its history and draw lessons from it. "Countries in the region, together with peace-loving forces within Japan, should unite in opposing militarism," he said. ■

articles.title: Poland Proposes European Legion With Ukrainian Veterans
articles.body:
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has advocated for the creation of a permanent European military structure, referred to as a “European Legion,” which could incorporate Ukrainian military personnel with combat experience following the conclusion of the war started by Russia.
Sikorski outlined the proposal during an interview with Ekathimerini, stating that the EU requires deeper military integration and autonomous defense capabilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I strongly advocate for a ‘European Legion’, a dedicated, standing force that could recruit seasoned professionals from the broader European family, including battle-hardened Ukrainian veterans after the war,” Sikorski said.
The minister argued that Europe must assume greater responsibility for its own security and reduce its reliance on US assistance during crises. He noted that Washington’s strategic focus is shifting toward the Indo-Pacific.
“We cannot call Washington every time there is a fire in our backyard – whether that is a conventional threat or Moscow weaponizing migration flows from Africa and the Middle East against the EU,” Sikorski stated.
Sikorski clarified that the proposed structure is not intended as an alternative to NATO or to duplicate its functions. Instead, he described it as a means to strengthen the European component within the alliance.
“The United States remains the indispensable anchor of our collective defense, but its role is evolving. America will continue to provide unmatched technological and intelligence capabilities, but Europe must do the heavy lifting on the ground,” he said.
Ukraine Claims Heavy Russian Losses, Successful Counteroffensive in South
Hybrid threats and Russian doctrine
During the interview, Sikorski also addressed the ongoing hybrid warfare tactics employed by Russia against NATO’s frontline states.
He stated that Russia is utilizing its military doctrine of “Maskirovka,” which involves strategic camouflage, disinformation, and orchestrated provocations.
Sikorski indicated that the Kremlin is conducting a campaign to fracture European societies through disinformation and state-sponsored sabotage, including assassination plots, arson, and drone incursions.
He referenced recent incidents, such as the violation of Polish airspace by a Russian cruise missile and previous attempts to sabotage railway infrastructure using contractors.
Poland reported a 140% increase in cyberattacks last year, totaling nearly 700,000 incidents, which Sikorski noted has prompted the country to enhance its cyber defense frameworks.
Poland’s military modernization
Sikorski’s comments coincide with Poland’s ongoing efforts to accelerate its military modernization program. On Saturday, Aug. 15, Poland hosted its largest-ever military parade in Warsaw to mark Armed Forces Day.
During the event, Prime Minister Donald Tusk emphasized that effective deterrence is a priority for the country, stating that “only those who are strong, well-prepared, truly independent and sovereign will avoid war.”
The parade featured more than 60 military aircraft and close to 2,000 Polish troops, alongside a display of new hardware, including US-designed F-35 fighter jets. A concurrent naval parade was held near the Baltic Sea cities of Gdynia and Gdańsk.
Poland allocated approximately 4.7% of its GDP to defense in 2025, the highest relative figure among NATO members, with a target of reaching 5% in 2026. The country aims to expand its armed forces to 500,000 service members, including 200,000 reservists, by 2039.

articles.title: US should avoid tensions with Russia ahead of elections — candidate for president
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, August 16. /TASS/. The administration of US President Donald Trump should avoid escalating tensions with Russia ahead of the midterm congressional elections and instead seek to expand trade and joint projects in the spirit of Anchorage, independent candidate for US President Diane Sare told TASS.
"Luckily, the United States is having midterm elections in November. The American people are weary of war, and this may impact the Trump administration's thinking on whether it is wise to escalate the conflict against Russia. Not to mention that, between arming Ukraine and Israel, and attacking Iran, we have depleted our own conventional munitions to very low levels," Sare said.
She announced in January that she would run as an independent candidate in the 2028 presidential election.
Sare called the US intelligence community and Pentagon providing Kiev with data for strikes on Russian territory "unfortunate and destructive." "It would be far more productive to revive the spirit of Alaska and emphasize the enormous benefits to be reaped on both sides by cooperation in trade and development on such projects as the Bering Strait Tunnel and the Northern Sea Transport Route," the presidential candidate said.
Sare said the US could immediately pledge not to be the first to use nuclear weapons, arguing that this "would help to alleviate some uncertainty and further the negotiating process." "Unfortunately, this is not what is being expressed by our Under Secretary of War for Policy, Elbridge Colby, who seems to be saying the opposite with regard to the use of tactical nuclear weapons," she said, referring to the Pentagon official’s remarks that the US "must carry the biggest stick in the world."
Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump met in Anchorage, Alaska, on August 15 last year. Putin later said the so-called spirit of Anchorage was not formalized in any documents or signed by either side. The summit focused on ways to end the conflict in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine report casualties in overnight drone, missile strikes
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
16 August 2026•Update: 16 August 2026
At least seven people were killed and 13 injured in Ukrainian drone attacks across Russia, while three people were killed and 23 injured in Russian strikes across Ukraine, officials on both sides said Sunday.
 
Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said in a statement on Russian social media platform Max that five civilians were killed in Ukrainian drone attacks as more than 150 drones were destroyed over three cities and nine districts of the region.
 
“The death toll from the enemy’s night attack has risen -- two more people have been found dead. They were discovered by rescuers. I express my deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims,” he said.
 
Slyusar added that multiple residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were damaged in the attack.
 
In a separate statement, Moscow region Governor Andrey Vorobyov said an 83-year-old man was killed when a drone fell on a private house in the Ramensky municipal district.
 
Meanwhile, acting Belgorod region Governor Aleksandr Shuvayev said a Ukrainian drone struck a bus carrying workers, killing a woman and injuring nine people.
 
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said around 600 drones had flown toward Moscow overnight, making it the largest attack on the capital in more than two years.
 
“The Defense Ministry air defense systems shot down nine more drones attacking Moscow. Three people in the area of the Moscow Ring Road were injured,” he said.
 
For his part, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram that two people were killed in Kryvyi Rih and another in Sumy, while six people were injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
 
“In Kryvyi Rih, two people died and 14 others were injured. There is one death in Sumy,” he said.
 
Earlier, the head of the Kryvyi Rih administration had reported one death and 13 injuries, indicating that casualty figures were still being updated.
 
Ukraine also continued strikes on Wildberries warehouses, with Vorobyov saying on Max that another facility caught fire at the Koledino industrial park in the city of Podolsk following a drone attack.
 
The attack also left 110 residential homes without electricity, according to Grigory Artamonov, head of the Podolsk urban district.
 
A separate logistics facility used to store medicines in Domodedovo caught fire and partially collapsed, with the damaged area estimated at 56,000 square meters (602,779 square feet), local authorities said.
 
More than 150 flights were either delayed or canceled at three Moscow airports -- Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo and Domodedovo -- amid the Ukrainian drone attack.
 
Both the Russian Defense Ministry and Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed carrying out overnight attacks.
 
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out a group strike using precision weapons and long-range drones against Ukrainian defense-industrial facilities in Kyiv, the Kremenchuk oil refinery in the Poltava region and metallurgical facilities in Kryvyi Rih.
 
The ministry said Kyiv-based enterprises produced components for Ukraine’s long-range Flamingo missiles and drones, while the Kryvyi Rih metallurgical complex produced steel for weapons and military equipment.
 
It also said a cargo ship carrying military supplies for Ukrainian forces was hit at the port of Odesa.
 
Ukraine’s General Staff, meanwhile, said its forces struck a Russian Bastion coastal missile complex in Crimea, hitting its launch positions and deployment site.
 
It added that a railway bridge near the settlement of Svitlodolynskyi in the Zaporizhzhia region was also hit.
 
Logistics and ammunition depots in Karlovka in the Donetsk region were also struck, it said.
 
Independent verification of the claims made by both sides remains difficult due to the ongoing conflict.

At least one person has been killed and three have been wounded in a Ukrainian drone barrage targeting Moscow, a local official says, as Russia has bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it destroyed 822 drones across the country overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin wrote on social media early on Sunday that the city was targeted with 600 drones and “201 drones were destroyed in Moscow region”.

At least five people were killed in attacks on southern Russia’s Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, according to regional authorities.
The drone assault came after Ukrainian authorities said late on Saturday that at least one person was killed and seven were wounded in Russian air attacks.
A woman was killed and six people were wounded in a missile and drone attack on Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in central Ukraine, the region’s governor said.
Officials in the capital said Kyiv was “under ballistic missile attack” late on Saturday, with at least one person wounded and fires sparked at nonresidential sites in the Obolonskyi and Holosiivskyi districts.
Defence and foreign policy analyst Pavel Felgenhauer told Al Jazeera that the targeting of capital cities suggests an escalation in the war. He noted that Ukraine had managed to bypass air defences in the Moscow region, which has the “best and most dense antiair defences in the entirety of Russia”. The attacks did not hit central Moscow but reached the outskirts of the capital, he added.
Separately, Romania’s Ministry of National Defence reported on Sunday that a Spanish F-18 jet on a NATO air policing mission to Romania had shot down a drone breaching its airspace.
Martin O’Donnell, a spokesman for NATO’s military headquarters, said the alliance is prepared to defend itself.
“Additional details regarding Sunday’s incident remain under investigation, but the drone appears to be Russian,” he said.
It was the fourth drone shot down in Romania this year.
The Defence Ministry wrote on social media that the drone came from neighbouring Moldova.
“The surveillance systems of the Ministry of National Defense detected the intrusion of an aerial target into national airspace, coming from the Republic of Moldova,” it said in a statement.
Romanian Defence Minister Radu Miruta congratulated the pilots and military personnel on what he called “a successful mission”.
In July, a Romanian jet shot down a suspected Russian drone, and in May, a stray drone injured two people in the Romanian city of Galati when it collided with a building.
Romania shares a 634km (394-mile) border with Ukraine and has repeatedly seen Russian drones breaching its airspace as Moscow escalates its bombing campaign against Ukrainian civilian and military infrastructure.
Escalating long-range strikes
Russia has maintained near-daily missile and drone strikes across Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in early 2022, and areas far from the front lines have frequently come under attack.
The war’s impact has also spread to key regional shipping routes with reports of mines and unmanned sea drones found floating in the Black Sea.
Civilian casualties in Ukraine hit their highest level since 2022 this July, with at least 437 killed and 2,610 injured, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted military, industrial and logistical facilities deep inside Russia, arguing its strikes are a response to Moscow’s ongoing bombardment of Ukrainian towns and infrastructure.

articles.title: Marco Rubio has unique power to promote peace in the world. Why isn’t he doing his job? | Simon Tisdall
articles.body:
Viewed from the state department in Washington DC, the world is on fire – but record heatwaves are not to blame. The unresolved Iran war has badly burned Donald Trump. His military campaign conclusively failed, energy and food prices are still rising, and a Republican rout in November’s midterm elections looms. Humiliatingly, Israel this week flatly rejected his latest Gaza peace proposals, days after Trump congratulated himself on a “historic breakthrough”. In Europe, Russia’s attacks on Nato allies grow increasingly brazen, threatening a wider escalation. The Ukraine war, which Trump vowed to end, is now well into its fifth year, with civilians on both sides caught in the killing fields. And these are just the bigger firestorms. There are plenty more.
Rarely has the need for effective, professional diplomacy been more pressing. So step forward Marco Rubio, US secretary of state and chief American diplomat. These are challenges that, if successfully tackled, could propel the 55-year-old son of Cuban immigrants and the former US senator for Florida into pole position in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. Here is a chance for Rubio to defy critics who dismiss him as a lickspittle and Trump dogsbody, and transform himself into respected global statesman. His boss mocked him as “little Marco” and a “loser” when they were election rivals in 2016. (Rubio called him a conman.) Now is Rubio’s opportunity to go big, be brave and prove he’s a winner.
Or maybe not.
Rubio is unlike recent US secretaries of state – heavyweights such as Hillary Clinton and Antony Blinken, or John Kerry, famed for his high-energy shuttle diplomacy. Rubio has little time for “peace processes”. Instead, he projects brute US power to impose take-it-or-leave-it “solutions” that advance US interests, as defined by Trump. It’s a modern form of imperialism. Target countries have a choice: become client states, like Venezuela and, prospectively, Cuba and Greenland, or be crushed. In Iran, the policy is not regime change, let alone democratic renewal. It’s regime compliance. Rubio behaves less like a peace-broker, more like a pith-helmeted colonial viceroy demanding fealty from obsequious satraps.
Speaking in Munich in February, Rubio aired his hawkishly retro doctrine of US primacy. He lamented the decline of “the great western empires … accelerated by godless communist revolutions and anti-colonial uprisings” and warned Europe faced “civilisational erasure”. The US didn’t want milksop allies “shackled by guilt and shame” about their imperial past, he said. “We want allies who are proud of their culture and heritage … and who, together with us, are willing and able to defend it.” Here was a familiar assertion of US hegemony, but one stripped of bogus altruism and pretence. It sounded a death knell for diplomacy. Trump has attacked eight countries in the past year. Cuba, Rubio’s obsession, could be next.
Rubio’s reluctance to get personally involved in peacemaking may be partly explained by his other, contradictory role, as Trump’s national security adviser. He has accepted the White House’s outsourcing of negotiations over Ukraine and Palestine to amateur envoys of limited ability – namely Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and business crony Steve Witkoff. Broadly speaking, Rubio has steered clear of direct involvement in the Iran talks, too, leaving JD Vance, the vice-president and his main potential rival in 2028, to take the flak. Rubio’s arm’s length approach smacks of calculation. Or maybe he’s just out of his depth. Maybe he has no clear idea what he, Marco, really thinks about any of these issues and simply does Trump’s erratic bidding.
This perception of a political chameleon lacking firm principles, consistent opinions and a strong moral compass is reinforced by his record. His biographer, Manuel Roig-Franzia, believes Rubio’s personal and political slipperiness – he once became a Mormon, then reverted to Catholicism – is rooted in a childhood need to belong, to be on the winning side, no matter the price. Senator Rubio was a China hawk. Now he toes Trump’s ingratiating line on Beijing. He used to castigate Russia; now he’s an appeaser. He championed overseas assistance but, in office, has gutted USAID and seeks to dismantle the international criminal court, a keystone of global order. He blasted Barack Obama’s Iran nuclear deal. Now he backs an accord that would offer additional concessions to Tehran. Accused by the Vatican of waging an immoral, unjust war, he travelled to Rome and set the pope straight.
The irony, or tragedy, of the Rubio conundrum is he has the power to do great good, if only he would stand up and be counted. Russia’s Vladimir Putin, losing on the battlefield and at home, is weaker than at any time since 2022. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy is short of missile interceptors, soldiers and political support. A ceasefire deal freezing the conflict is there for the making by the only country – the US – that can meaningfully squeeze both sides. Likewise, in Israel, the architect of the Gaza genocide and disastrous wars with Hamas, Iran and Hezbollah – Benjamin Netanyahu – faces defeat in October’s elections. Here’s a rare opportunity to quietly shelve Trump’s Board of Peace idiocies, halt Jewish settler violence in the West Bank and make a fresh, inclusive start based on UN resolutions.
Rubio could also do the Middle East, the global economy, American consumers and himself a power of good by taking charge of moribund peace talks with Iran and resuscitating the June memorandum of understanding that Tehran insists is the only route out of the strait of Hormuz logjam. In doing so, Rubio would have the enthusiastic backing of most Americans, European and Gulf state governments, energy producers and businesses, and Maga supporters who rightly fear Trump has dragged the US into another forever war. Even Trump may be grateful. He knows he’s in a hole. He needs someone to dig him out.
The fact that Rubio, despite his ostensibly uniquely powerful position, is unlikely to do any of the above marks him out as the most dangerous man in the US administration after Trump himself. He is dangerous because he enables and facilitates Trump’s worst instincts – and neglects his duty. He is dangerous because he provides pseudo-intellectual respectability to far-right fantasies about unfettered US supremacy. More so than the impetuous Vance, indulging in puerile name-calling on social media, and the “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth, a ranting ultra-nationalist, Rubio is dangerous because he can look and sound reasonable. He stands a fair chance of becoming Trump’s chosen successor and heir to the Maga brand.
Maybe, before that happens, he will change again. Maybe he will rediscover a few principles, find a diplomatic backbone, extinguish a few fires. He has shown repeatedly that his views are infinitely fungible. Rubio could yet do great things. Or he could become a problem as great or greater than Trump.
- 
  Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

articles.title: Mass drone attack on Moscow as Russian strikes kill three in Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian rescuers use a water hose as they work to extinguish a fire at the site of a Russian strike in Kyiv on August 16, 2026. (AFP photo)
Hundreds of drones targeted Moscow on Aug. 16 as Russia launched missile strikes that killed three people and wounded more than a dozen in Kiev and other Ukrainian cities, officials on the two sides said.
Amid the intense hostilities, three people were also killed in the Russian city of Rostov, while a Spanish NATO fighter jet shot down a drone that crossed into Romanian territory — the second time in two days that the war has spilled over into eastern Europe.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported a sustained overnight drone assault on the capital, issuing a string of updates over several hours.
Air defenses intercepted more than 600 drones headed towards Moscow, with around 200 which were shot down in the region, according to his statements on the state-backed MAX platform.
Moscow regional governor Andrey Vorobyov described the assault as "one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory", adding that six people were wounded in the region.
"In Podolsk, a UAV hit caused a fire at a Wildberries warehouse in the Koledino Industrial Park," Vorobyov added.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted warehouses linked to the Wildberries online retailer, arguing its strikes are a response to Moscow's bombardment of Ukrainian towns and infrastructure.
Since mid-July, Ukraine has struck around 20 Wildberries warehouses and buildings.
Russia's missile strikes killed two people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region with another fatality in Kryvyi Rig, President Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown. More than 20 people were wounded across Kiev, Brovary, Kryvyi Rig, Odesa, and Dnipetrovsk.
Russian forces hit two industrial sites in Kryvyi Rig, local defense council head Oleksandr Vilkul said on Telegram.
In Kiev, authorities issued an air raid alert just before 2:00 am (2300 GMT) and several explosions were heard shortly after.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Kiev was "under ballistic missile attack" and urged residents to remain in shelters.
The strikes sparked fires in the Obolonsky and Holosiivskyi districts of the capital.
Kremenchuk in the central Poltava region also came under attack, local officials said, without providing details of damage or casualties.
Russia has maintained near-daily missile and drone strikes across Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in early 2022. Zelensky has said Ukraine's increasing attacks deep inside Russia, on refineries as well as the warehouses, aim to undermine Russia's war economy.
Romania's defense ministry said that a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone that breached its airspace near the border with Ukraine and Moldova. Debris fell in an unpopulated area of the Galati region, near the Ukrainian border, it added, though it was not known where the drone came from.
Countries bordering the conflict have faced increasing spillovers from the drone war between Ukraine and Russia. NATO said on Aug. 14 that its fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace. It was the second time in a week that a drone had been shot down in Latvian airspace, the country's defense ministry said.
In July, Romania expelled a Russian embassy employee in what it called "a firm response" to drones repeatedly breaching the country's airspace.
Romania shot down three drones on three consecutive days before the expulsion.

articles.title: Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
articles.body:
Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
August 16, 2026
In late 2024, North Korea sent troops to help defend the Kursk region of Russia from Ukraine. International officials estimate that 14,000-15,000 North Korean troops were initially deployed to assist Russia in its war in Ukraine..
Now, Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect that North Korea is planning to send an additional 30,000-50,000 troops to Russia. Ukrainian officials have also stated that North Korean ballistic missiles are being fired from Russia.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has raised concerns that North Korea's improved combat and weapons experience could pose a security threat to Ukraine, as well as the Asia-Pacific region.
Defense in Russia
Observers have had mixed responses to Zelenskyy's remarks. Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military and political expert at the Ukrainian Center for Security Studies, told DW that new troops from North Korea would likely be used to secure Russia's border territories. Aside from remaining in Kursk, North Korean soldiers could also help secure southwestern Vornezh.
"These forces could free up Russian occupational forces," Kovalenko said. "Russia would then be able to deploy around 15,000 troops to battles along front lines in Vovchansk, Kharkiv, Sumy or even Chernihiv."
Kovalenko does not expect North Korean troops to fight on Ukrainian territory.
The Russian military analyst Ruslan Leviev agrees. "It's one thing to recapture Russian territory," he told DW, "and an entirely different thing to be present on internationally recognized Ukrainian territory, taking part in a war of aggression."
"Diplomatically speaking," he said, "those are two entirely different concepts."
Russia not outgunned
Leviev said he had not seen concrete evidence of a noteworthy North Korean presence in Russia. He said Moscow had enough troops available without having to draw foreign soldiers into the fight.
"If you look at the front line, you can see that Russia's forces have been fairly active since mid-July," Leviev said. "That's a clear sign they still have enough forces."
Estimates by the economist Janis Kluge, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), back this up. "While Russia's recruitment campaign has shown signs of strain this year, regional spending figures indicate that Russia is still recruiting around 1,000 contract soldiers each day," he recently wrote in a report.
Intelligence on North Korea's short- and medium-range ballistic systems, the KN-23 and KN-24, is far less speculative. Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) states that North Korea has delivered 148 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles since 2025.
In July, Zelenskyy said one such missile had struck a home near Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih, killing two parents and three children.
The HUR recently reported that a North Korean missile unit was deploying to Russia's Voronezh region, where it could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has taken this as indication that Russia's strategic reserve is depleted.
Kovalenko has come to a different conclusion. Instead of having run out of reserves, he said, he believes that Russia is looking to launch a higher number of missiles "to spread more terror."
'Instruments of terror'
Ukrainian military sources say North Korean missiles are similar to Russia's Iskander missiles, but with a greater payload, longer range and lower accuracy.
The military expert Yuri Fyodorov calls North Korea's missiles "instruments of terror." He told DW that "it is very difficult to hit a small target with North Korean weapons." He said he believed that Russia had deliberately targeted residential areas with these missiles.
Like the Russian Iskander 9M723, KN-23 and KN-24 missiles can only be stopped by US-made Patriot air-defense systems, which Ukraine has run critically low on.
Leviev said ballistic missiles would play a key role in this phase of the war. As Ukraine's stockpiles run low, he said, it will become a growing priority to Russia to keep a steady supply.
This summer, Leviev said, he has seen Russia launch far more ballistic missiles than in previous years. Should Russia's missile supply run low by winter, he said, "there will still be North Korea reserves, to make sure Ukraine cannot catch its breath."
No turning point
None of the experts DW spoke with believes that North Korea's involvement will bring about a turning point in Russia's war with Ukraine.
Jenny Town, of the US-based Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the time had passed for North Korea's involvement to make a significant difference. Instead, she said, Russia and North Korea have established a mutually beneficial partnership that is only likely to deepen through the course of the war with Ukraine.
Kovalenko also doesn't expect Russia to make substantial territorial gains along the front lines, but he is concerned about the upcoming winter. "October, November and December could become very trying for Ukraine," he said.
Russian forces could benefit from a possible new military call up, from freeing up fighters it replaces with North Korean troops and from a further stream of ballistic missiles. "That would be no good for the course of the war, and for Ukraine's war interests," Fyodorov said.
This article was originally written in Russian.

articles.title: Ukraine launches one of the largest aerial attacks on Russia yet
articles.body:
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones into Russia in one of the largest aerial attacks of the war
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones across Russia Sunday, killing at least six people in one of Kyiv's largest aerial attacks of the war.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said that it had destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones overnight. Some 600 drones were detected headed toward the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, with a third destroyed over the Moscow region itself.
An 83-year-old man was killed after a Ukrainian drone hit a private home in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said. He also confirmed that a Ukrainian attack had sparked a blaze at a warehouse belonging to Russian retail giant Wildberries in the town of Podolsk, where images shared by Russian media outlets showed columns of black smoke.
A drone attack targeted three towns in Russia's southwestern Rostov region, killing five people, local Gov. Yury Slyusar said. The attack, with more than 150 drones, damaged several homes and a railway station and sparked a forest fire.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Russia this year, with long-range missiles and swarms of drones increasingly targeting military industries and energy facilities. It has also increasingly pummeled giant Wildberries depots, burning billions of dollars' worth of merchandise and bringing the war home to the Russian public nearly 4½ years into Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A Russian missile attack on Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 14 others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media Sunday. He also said that one more person had been killed in the city of Sumy.
Meanwhile, a Russian attack on Kyiv sparked fires throughout the Ukrainian capital and injured six people.
"Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure," Zelenskyy said. "Since this morning, air raid alerts have continued in many regions – the Russians launched another wave of drones."

articles.title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill 7, injure 51 as Kyiv hit in overnight barrage; drone downed over Romania
articles.body:

Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least seven civilians and injured 51 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Aug. 16.

articles.title: Russia’s air defense leans on a few “flying quarterback” jets
articles.body:
- Analyst Michael Bohnert says Russia has roughly half a dozen operational A-50U early warning aircraft, with no new airframes built since 1992 and no A-100 replacement in serial production.
- Analysts estimate Russia has roughly half a dozen operational A-50U aircraft, with no new airframes built since 1992 and the A-100 replacement still not in serial production.
Russia’s A-50U airborne early warning aircraft function as “flying quarterbacks” for its air defense network, and Moscow has no near-term way to replace the ones it has lost, defense researcher Michael Bohnert wrote in a recent analysis of the fleet.
Bohnert said the aircraft’s value comes down to line of sight and the curvature of the Earth. A ground-based radar can typically see a low-flying object only 10 to 20 miles away before the horizon blocks it, he said, while an airborne radar can potentially detect the same target from more than 200 miles out.
“This has two major implications,” Bohnert wrote. “The first is it provides much earlier warning. Up to an hour for a strike drone and 10 to 30 minutes for a cruise missile. The second is it covers a much larger area easily replacing a dozen or more surface radars.”
Because a single A-50U can substitute for numerous ground radars, Bohnert said Russia can leave many of those systems switched off until they are needed to target an incoming missile. A radar that is turned off, he noted, is much harder to locate because it emits no signal for enemy sensors to detect. He added that the same line-of-sight advantage extends to communications, since A-50U crews are trained to control both air and ground assets and can see and talk to nearly everything within range.
On why Russia cannot quickly rebuild the fleet, Bohnert said the last A-50 airframe was produced around 1992, and that despite periodic upgrades, the type has been out of production for decades. The base Il-76 airframe is still manufactured today, he said, but the radar system requires specialized structural reinforcements that are far harder to produce. Russia’s intended successor, the A-100, has still not entered serial production after more than a decade of development, according to Bohnert, who said the aircraft’s radar is expensive to build and depends on numerous specialized parts.
In 2025, Ukraine struck a facility involved in A-100 production using FP-1 drones, destroying a test aircraft and damaging the factory. Bohnert said work on the program has likely been on hold since, and that new aircraft are unlikely to arrive for several years.
Bohnert estimated Russia currently has around half a dozen operational A-50U aircraft, used mainly to protect Russian President Vladimir Putin and only occasionally to help Russian forces fend off increasingly frequent Ukrainian FP-1 drone and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile attacks. He pointed to Ukraine’s use of UK-supplied Storm Shadow missiles at near-maximum range inside Russian territory as an indicator of how far back from the front line the A-50U fleet is being kept.
Flight-tracking data compiled separately by the open-source channel CyberBoroshno points to the same conclusion: a small, closely guarded fleet flown under increasing pressure. The channel analyzed more than 1,600 messages referencing the A-50U between June 4 and August 2 and found the aircraft largely grounded for duty against Ukraine through June 22, aside from the return to service of a repaired airframe, tail number “47 red,” and transit flights between Vorkuta and Olenya.
Starting June 23, one aircraft began flying nearly every night over what the channel called Russia’s Volga rear area, covering Ulyanovsk and Samara regions, a pattern CyberBoroshno said held for the rest of the period and totaled roughly 60 individual sorties. The channel said an A-50U played a decisive role in repelling a Ukrainian cruise missile strike on July 4. Flights that had previously originated from Ivanovo, described as the fleet’s home base, and from Ulyanovsk largely stopped after that date, with operations dispersing to Bolshoye Savino near Perm, Orenburg-2 and Chelyabinsk, which the channel attributed to an effort to protect a scarce asset once its effectiveness became clear.
On July 7, Russia had four A-50U aircraft airborne simultaneously, which CyberBoroshno said represented nearly the entire operational fleet and a readiness level it had not previously recorded. The channel also reported one aircraft flying continuous night duty for five straight days, including a shift from 2:45 to 4:45 a.m. during which Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo missiles were in the air; Samara, one of the areas the missiles reached that night, fell within that aircraft’s coverage zone at the time.
Confirmed losses to date remain limited but are rising. The open-source monitoring project Oryx has visually confirmed the destruction of at least two A-50 aircraft and one Beriev A-100LL flying laboratory, the testbed used to develop the A-100’s radar, a figure Oryx’s methodology treats as a floor rather than a full count, since it requires photographic or video evidence for each loss.

US top Middle East commander visits deployed aircraft carrier, and other Mideast news
Adm. Brad Cooper, the top U.S. military commander in the Middle East, visited the USS Lincoln in the Arabian Sea during a 10-day tour in the region that concluded on Saturday, U.S. Central Command said.
Israel said its strikes in southern Lebanon, which killed at least 11 people, targeted two Hezbollah commanders. And a Hamas delegation is in Cairo on Sunday for Gaza ceasefire-related talks with Egyptian officials.
Here’s a look at the latest developments on Sunday in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
US Central Command chief visits aircraft carrier
Adm. Cooper visited the USS Lincoln in the Arabian Sea as reports have emerged of mental health and supply issues aboard the long-deployed aircraft carrier. The Lincoln arrived in the Middle East in January and has been supporting the U.S. war against Iran, including the blockade on Iranian ports. Its deployment has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days.
Extended deployments of carriers – which can have more than 5,000 sailors and Marines on board – have raised concerns about the impact not only on the ships but on service members.
“History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era,” Cooper said of the Lincoln strike group in a statement released Saturday.
Cooper also went to Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates to meet with civilian and military leaders, according to the Central Command statement.
Israel targets two Hezbollah commanders in Saturday’s strikes
Israel’s military said it targeted two Hezbollah commanders in strikes in southern Lebanon on Saturday, in the deadliest attacks since a truce between Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah went into effect in June.
Lebanon’s Health Ministry and state news agency said at least 11 people were killed in two strikes – one on a home on the edge of Ansar village where seven people died, and another on the village of Deir al-Zahrani, where four were killed.
Israel’s military said early on Sunday morning that the latter strike killed Abu Hassan Alaa, whom it described as a “senior commander” for Hezbollah who had taken part in attacks against Israel’s soldiers in southern Lebanon as well as led militants who targeted Israeli soldiers and civilians over several years.
Earlier, Israel’s military had said the strike on Ansar killed Ali Samir Al-Haj Hassan, whom it described as a battalion commander with Hezbollah’s elite Radwan Force unit. The military said Haj Hassan’s family was with him, but emphasized that the family was not targeted.
The United States has been mediating talks between Israel and the Lebanese government.
On Saturday, Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam criticized Israel’s airstrikes. The office of Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Hezbollah violated the ceasefire by attacking Israeli soldiers inside Lebanon, seriously wounding three. It added the military responded by striking the Hezbollah headquarters, which ordered the attack, learning only later that Hezbollah “deliberately put civilians” in that military compound.
Hamas delegation is in Cairo for Gaza ceasefire talks
A Hamas delegation, chaired by the group’s leader Khalil al-Hayya, is in Cairo Sunday for Gaza ceasefire-related talks with Egyptian officials, the group said.
The talks come as mediators push for the implementation of a roadmap to move forward with U.S. President Donald Trump’s peace plan, which calls for the disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups in Gaza, the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the area as well as handing over power to Palestinian technocrats.
Israel’s Netanyahu has rejected Trump’s latest plan to advance the stalled ceasefire in Gaza, saying Israel will not withdraw from any of the roughly 60% of the territory it controls until Hamas has been completely disarmed — something the militant group controlling the other 40% has long resisted.
It wasn’t immediately clear whether al-Hayya would meet with Trump’s son-in-law and negotiator Jared Kushner, the Board of Peace’s high representative Nickolay Mladenov, or executive board member and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who are scheduled to travel to Israel and Egypt this week.
Iran says Qatar is holding 3 of its pilots
Qatar’s armed forces captured and are holding three Iranian pilots who went missing in March when their jets were downed, the Missing Persons Committee of Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff said. Qatar, however, denied it.
Iran’s state TV reported on Sunday that the committee’s commander responded by urging Qatar to allow Iranian Air Force experts to conduct a field investigation.
Saturday’s statement alleged that Qatar had not allowed the pilots to meet or communicate with families or Iranian officials handling their cases. A spokesperson with Qatar’s foreign ministry, Majed Al Ansari, denied the claims and indicated on X that the pilots had been shot down and that Qatar’s search and rescue teams found the remains of one.
