articles.title: Why Iran’s threat keeps haunting the Middle East - and how to finally break the cycle - opinion
articles.body:
For nearly 50 years, the world has dealt with Iran under a straightforward premise: the sole source of danger is the theocracy installed by the 1979 revolution.
Western policies have split between containing the regime, changing its conduct, eroding its capabilities, or waiting for internal collapse. The record of these tactics, though, raises a tougher question.
Why does the Iranian threat return each time Tehran’s foes believe they have contained it?
The breeding grounds enabling centralized power
For decades, the world may have fixated on who governs Iran while ignoring the framework that lets central authorities rebuild their power project whenever conditions change.
The core issue is about more than the nuclear program, ballistic missile stockpile, and proxy networks. These are assets that can be disabled or partly destroyed.
They spring, however, from a large state with a huge population, energy reserves, a scientific and industrial foundation, geographic reach, and military institutions honed across decades.
Lost facilities, leaders, and munitions cannot wipe out technical know-how or erase recovery capacity. A single tool may break, but the underlying machine still can build a replacement.
History shows international dealings with Iran have targeted what can be destroyed; capabilities can be degraded. But such tactics leave unanswered the more fundamental question of how to stop a large, centralized state with people, resources and expertise from rebuilding losses once conditions ease.
So, the issue moves from disarmament to state structure, from who governs Iran to how power sources inside the country are administered.
One episode lays bare this disconnect. The July 2015 nuclear deal capped portions of Iran’s nuclear work. It left Tehran’s view of its regional standing intact. Missile work and proxy operations also proceeded without pause.
The January 2020 killing of Maj.-Gen. Qasem Soleimani jolted the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, although influence networks resumed activity once roles were reassigned.
Strikes on Iranian military sites have proved able to inflict damage and disrupt operations, but they cannot ensure permanent disablement.
Containment thus amounts to little more than managing repeated rounds of buildup, strike and rearmament.
Viewed this way, regime change in Iran offers at best a partial fix if presented as a final answer to the problem. The ruling system provides the country’s power project with its ideology, while the centralized state furnishes its resources and wealth.
Replacing the regime while leaving power administration untouched may soften rhetoric but offers no assurance of a different course. A more pragmatic, economy-focused government could emerge.
Geography, national interests and latent capabilities, however, survive leadership turnover. Long-held regional ambitions would likely resurface, framed in nationalist rather than revolutionary terms.
That said, casting the Iranian state as inherently hostile misreads reality. Most countries adjust conduct when their institutions, military doctrine, and balance between rulers and ruled evolve.
The objective is something other than indefinite weakening of Iran. It is blocking the convergence of unchecked central power, expansionist ideology, and exclusive control over military decisions.
Chaotic breakup of the Iranian state carries its own severe risks. Internal diversity, widespread weapons, and Iran’s strategic position could turn collapse into civil conflict, foreign meddling, and massive disruption of energy flows and shipping lanes.
Break the ‘buildup, strike, resurgence’ pattern
The most durable course therefore starts inside Iran, on the premise that Iranians alone hold the right to choose their governing system and its structure.
Broad decentralization or federalism, and possibly confederal arrangements if adopted through national consent and constitutional agreement, can curb the center’s monopoly on wealth and decisions, give regions greater say over resources and fiscal matters, and write institutional limits into the use of national capacities for foreign ventures.
Forcing such models from outside, by contrast, would let authorities cast themselves as defenders of national unity and turn reform into a pretext for harsher repression.
Decentralization hardly guarantees Iran will turn automatically into a peaceful country. Constitutional arrangements by themselves cannot dispel national ambitions or remove foreign frictions. Their worth lies in raising the price of decision monopolization, spreading oversight of resources, and making long-term foreign ventures far harder to pursue without broad consent and accountability.
Such rules constrain impulsive action while still falling short of an ironclad promise of responsible behavior.
No global requirement exists for a permanent Iranian adversary to justify alliances and defense budgets. Removing the regime with no plan for what follows promises an even more dangerous crisis.
What is required instead is ending the threat’s ability to regenerate, through four parallel steps: capping offensive capabilities, advancing institutional reform that disperses power inside Iran, upholding regional deterrence to block coercion, and pursuing diplomacy that links economic and political integration to revised conduct.
The world has repeatedly slowed Iran’s power project. It has never eliminated the country’s ability to rebuild it. The ruling system may fall one day, but its collapse would leave intact the building blocks of Iranian strength.
If a framework survives that lets central authorities marshal people, resources and expertise behind foreign ventures, any win will amount to a temporary pause between rounds.
A credible resolution comes when Iran’s strength changes from a source of fear for neighbors into a force bounded by institutions and directed by societal interests. Only then does the root problem resolve itself. The danger will not have sustained another setback – it will have lost the conditions that kept reviving it.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

articles.title: Russian Strikes Devastate Metinvest’s Zaporizhstal Factory, Epicentr Mall in Zaporizhzhia
articles.body:
Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia have severely damaged two major Ukrainian businesses, forcing a complete shutdown of Metinvest’s Zaporizhstal steel plant and destroying an Epicentr shopping center. Seven workers were killed and 21 others were injured in the early morning attacks on Aug. 11 and Aug. 12 respectively.
Overnight Aug. 10-11, Russian forces launched a ballistic missile attack on the Metinvest industrial complex, which occurred as workers were heading to a bomb shelter immediately after the alarm went off, the parent company Metinvest said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The attack directly struck essential facilities in Zaporizhstal’s coke and blast furnace divisions, destroying power units and critical grid infrastructure. With its core iron and coking power severed, the metallurgical giant was forced to completely shut down its blast furnaces, the company said.
The attack is a major blow to Ukraine’s heavy industry as the plant had already reported a net loss of Hr. 1.06 billion ($25.7 million) for the first half of 2026, down from Hr. 1.37 billion profit in the same period last year. Other regional Metinvest facilities are operating at reduced capacity while specialists assess repair timelines.
Founded in 1933, Zaporizhstal is one of the largest metallurgical companies in Ukraine and is part of Rinat Akhmetov’s Metinvest Group. The plant exports steel products to more than 50 countries and has an annual production capacity of 4 million tons of pig iron, 3.6 million tons of hot-rolled steel and 1.2 million tons of cold-rolled steel.
Ukraine Claims Heavy Russian Losses, Successful Counteroffensive in South
Early on Aug. 12, Russian strikes targeted an Epicentr shopping center in a residential district of Zaporizhzhia, triggering a massive fire, Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration head Ivan Fedorov reported.
The strike was the latest blow to Epicentr, Ukraine’s largest home improvement retailer. Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Russian attacks have destroyed 417,000 square meters of Epicentr’s retail space and damaged a further 500,000 square meters, causing billions of dollars in losses to goods and infrastructure.
Epicentr K was founded by Oleksandr and Halyna Hereha in 2003, when the company opened its first home improvement store in Kyiv. The chain currently operates 72 shopping centers across Ukraine, with a total retail area of more than 2 million square meters (21.5 million square feet) and around 38,000 employees. Approximately 4,600 of its employees are currently serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

articles.title: Iran, US trade threats; Israel bombs Lebanon for second day
articles.body:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in the Middle East.
Here are the key events on Sunday morning:
• Iran and the US are continuing to sabre-rattle over the Strait of Hormuz. Trump on Saturday claimed he could declare the strategic waterway a "territory of the United States" while a senior Iranian diplomat told the US to "accept the reality of defeat".
• The threats come ahead of Monday's deadline under the June Islamabad agreement, which gave the US and Iran two months to reach an understanding on reopening the key waterway.
• Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Oman over the strait are continuing but that re-opening the waterway is a "completely separate matter" that will depend on the US meeting Tehran's conditions.
• Qatar has denied claims by Iran that it is holding three pilots captured during a combat mission earlier in the war.
• Meanwhile, Israel has threatened to further escalate attacks on Lebanon, a day after killing at least 11 people in one of the heaviest rounds of strikes since the ceasefire came into effect in June.
Houthis launch new attacks on Yemen port city of Mocha
Yemeni government forces said Sunday that Houthi fighters have launched new missile and drone attacks on the port city of Mocha.
Air defences had intercepted a drone fired by the group, they said.
The director of Mocha port said Saturday it has been forced to suspend operations after being hit by more than 25 missiles in recent days.
The recent attacks have raised fears that Yemen could be sliding back into civil war, four years after a ceasefire ended the conflict between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognised government.
The head of Iran's parliamentary national security committee, Ebrahim Azizi, has mocked Trump over his latest threats to take over the Strait of Hormuz.
"The US President ought to worry about his own security rather than his endless bluffing regarding the Strait of Hormuz; before he ends up hiding in a food truck," Azizi wrote on X on Saturday.
He was referring to reports in US media that Trump hid in a catering truck to leave Air Force One during a recent visit to Turkey following concerns about an Iranian attack.
Iran executes man over involvement in January protests
Iran's judiciary announced the execution on Sunday of a man who was convicted of running over several police officers with his car during anti-government protests in January.
"Shahram Sadeghi, sentenced to death for having carried out an operational action in support of the Zionist regime and the United States, was executed this morning," the judiciary's Mizan Online website said.
It added that the man had run over several police officers with his car on 8 January in Karaj, west of Tehran, wounding seven of them.
A protest movement initially sparked in late December by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 January.
Israel threatens escalation in Lebanon amid new strike
Lebanese media reported a new Israeli attack in the south on Sunday shortly after Israel's defence minister Israel Katz vowed to continue strikes.
Lebanon's National News Agency reported in a strike in Majdal Zoun on Sunday morning, a day after at least 11 people were killed in the heaviest Israeli attacks since the US-brokered ceasefire came into effect in June.
"No account in any arena will remain open. We will defend our soldiers and civilians with force," Katz wrote on X.
Medics at the site of an Israeli strike in Deir al-Zahrani, 15 August 2026. [Getty]
Iran disputes Qatar, Kuwait accounts of captured pilots
An Iranian military official said on Sunday that Qatar should allow an Iranian team to enter the country to investigate the fate of pilots whom Tehran says were captured by Qatari forces, Iranian media reported.
Qatar denies holding any Iranian pilots. Doha said on Saturday that its search and rescue teams had found the remains of one pilot after Iranian aircraft violated Qatari airspace in March and failed to respond to attempts to contact them.
Qatar said it had contacted Iran to coordinate the handover of the remains and had invited Tehran to review details of its search and rescue operations, but had received no response.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff, said an Iranian Air Force expert and fact-finding team had been waiting for months to enter Qatar, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
He accused Qatari officials of repeatedly delaying the investigation and preventing the pilots' return to Iran. He called for the International Committee of the Red Cross to urgently follow up on the case.

articles.title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,467,320 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022

Russia has lost around 1,467,320 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 16.
The figure includes 1,510 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,270 tanks, 25,151 armored combat vehicles, 134,851 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,007 artillery systems, 2,034 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,570 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 463,404 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,257 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

articles.title: Iran says Qatar delaying probe into fate of Iranian pilots, Tasnim news agency
articles.body:
Iran accuses Qatar of thwarting probe into fate of pilots
- Iran said the airmen have been held since March 2 when their fighter jets were shot down.
- Qatar denies holding the pilots, saying it invited Iran for briefings on rescue efforts but that Tehran did not respond.
- The incident ties into a wider Middle East conflict involving US and Israeli attacks on Iran, with ongoing tensions and failed peace talks.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran accused Qatar on Aug 16 of thwarting efforts to work out what happened to three pilots Tehran says were captured during the Middle East war, though the Gulf state has denied detaining them.
Iran previously reported that one pilot was killed and others missing after a sortie to Qatar in March, but did not claim at the time that any of them was captured.
“A team of experts from the Iranian Air Force has been waiting for several months to travel to Qatar to conduct an on-site investigation,” said Iranian General Mohammad Bagherzadeh.
“However, due to persistent delays by Qatari authorities, the return of our brave pilots to their homeland remains impossible,” he added, according to the Tasnim news agency.
He called on Doha to authorise the team to travel to Qatar.
Bagherzadeh accused Qatar on Aug 15 of having captured three Iranian pilots who were carrying out an operation against the United States’ Al Udeid air base in early March and demanded their release.
Qatar denied holding the pilots and said an invitation was sent to Iran “to be briefed on the details of the search & rescue operations in April, but the Iranian side has yet to respond”.
Iran’s military said in July it retrieved the body of pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during the attack on Al Udeid.
The largest US military base in the Middle East, Al Udeid hosts forward elements of US Central Command, as well as its air and special operations forces.
In early March, Qatar’s Defence Ministry said it shot down two Iranian Sukhoi Su-24 bombers.
It was not immediately clear whether they were the same aircraft referred to by Iran, as Qatar and other countries across the region faced retaliatory attacks following the US and Israeli strikes that triggered the war.
It was the first time a Gulf country reported shooting down an Iranian aircraft since the war broke out on Feb 28.
The Middle East war broke out when the US and Israel attacked Iran, which retaliated with attacks across the region.
Diplomatic efforts led to an April ceasefire that ended nearly 40 days of fighting, followed by the signing of a framework for peace talks in June that later collapsed.
Iran and the US have since traded fire sporadically, with fighting mainly centred in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Qatar, which took part in mediation efforts to end the fighting, came under fire after the truce broke down, reporting attacks on its territory and at least one Qatari tanker transiting the strait. AFP

articles.title: Ukrainian rapper mocked Russia’s claim he helped deliver drones for attacks near Moscow. A month later, Russia allegedly tried to kill him in Poland
articles.body:
On 14 August 2026, Polish broadcaster RMF FM identified American-Ukrainian rapper and video blogger Kyivstoner as the previously unnamed target of an alleged Russian-directed assassination plot in Warsaw. The case comes as European authorities investigate suspected Russian attacks and sabotage across the continent.
The alleged plot against Kyivstoner comes amid attacks on Kremlin critics abroad, including the fatal shooting of a Russian opposition artist in Poland in June.
Polish authorities disclosed the Kyivstoner's case on 13 August but withheld the target’s identity. RMF’s identification points to a possible motive, though it relies on unverified allegations from the FSB, Russia's domestic security agency that Kyivstoner of managed drone deliveries intended for attacks near Moscow.
Who is Kyivstoner?
Kyivstoner was born Albert Vasiliev and uses the name Slevin Dadyan on his US passport. He gained attention through humorous videos and the Ukrainian group Hryby before releasing solo tracks, including “Leto” (Summer) and “Zvuk” (Sound).
In a 2025 interview, Vasiliev voiced support for Ukrainians and opposition to Russian occupation, saying Russian ruler Vladimir Putin made him angry and that he wanted civilians and soldiers to stop dying.
In July 2026, Russia’s FSB accused Kyivstoner of overseeing logistics for a foiled drone attack on a defense enterprise near Moscow.
The agency alleged that 35 drones assembled in Kyiv were concealed in a shipment of ceramic tiles and smuggled into Russia through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus. Russian authorities also added Vasiliev to a register of people they label as involved in extremist or terrorist activity.
Vasiliev responded on Instagram by mocking Russia's allegation, saying he had been relaxing and playing video games rather than organizing an attack.
Russian authorities also accuse him of cooperating with Ukrainian intelligence. He denies the accusations, and RMF offered no independent evidence to substantiate them.
Suspect detained before alleged attack
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Polish services detained the Russian suspect on 7 August, stopping the alleged attack “at the last minute.” US services assisted the operation. A Polish court remanded the man in custody for three months.
The journalists described the Russian citizen as a native of Donbas in eastern Ukraine. Tusk said the target, who holds Ukrainian and US passports, was “inconvenient to the Putin regime.”
The prime minister called it the first Russian-ordered attempt of its kind against a US citizen in another NATO country.
Killings and disrupted plots across Europe
Throughout Europe, Russia has tried to hunt down and kill anti-Kremlin critics and supporters of Ukraine. In June, Russian opposition artist Robert Kuzovkov, known as Semyon Skrepetsky, was shot dead in eastern Poland. Hours earlier, he had reported threats from “Russian patriots.” Polish authorities detained two Belarusian nationals, but have not attributed the killing to Moscow.
US and German services also reportedly foiled a Russian plot against Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger in 2024. German intelligence later treated the surveillance of Bavarian drone manufacturer Donaustahl’s CEO as a suspected planned assassination.

Ukrainian forces struck a Russian air defense system, military storage facilities, and two command posts across temporarily occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia regions, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 15.

According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Strela-10 short-range surface-to-air missile system in temporarily occupied Kreminna, Luhansk region.
The Strela-10 is a Soviet-designed mobile air defense system mounted on a tracked armored vehicle and designed to protect ground forces from low-flying aircraft, helicopters, and other aerial targets at short ranges.
A Russian drone storage facility in temporarily occupied Vuhledar, Donetsk region, was also hit. In temporarily occupied Lysychansk, Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces targeted a depot containing logistical and material supplies used by Russian troops.
Two Russian command posts were among the other targets. The General Staff identified their locations as temporarily occupied Selydove in the Donetsk region and temporarily occupied Mykhailivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the extent of the damage and the final results of the strikes were still being assessed.
The strikes came as Ukrainian forces continued operations against Russian military and defense-industrial facilities both in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories and inside Russia.
On August 15, Ukrainian forces also struck the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara and the Savasleyka military airfield in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region. The Houthi group launched a new wave of drone and missile attacks in Mocha and Marib in southwestern Yemen as escalation continues to rise in the war-torn Arab country, according to pro-government forces and local media on Sunday.
The National Resistance Forces, aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and led by Presidential Leadership Council member Tariq Saleh, said one missile hit Mocha, without giving details about injuries or damage.
In Marib, the provincial government’s media office said six ballistic missiles and four drones targeted residential neighborhoods in the city Saturday evening, injuring four people and causing damage to homes and civilian property.

The media office called on the international community to “condemn these attacks and crimes targeting displacement camps, residential neighborhoods and civilian facilities, and document them as violations of international humanitarian law.”
The Houthis have not yet commented on the report.
Mocha and Marib have come under repeated Houthi attacks in recent days amid mounting escalation across the war-torn country.
Yemen has witnessed a relative lull since April 2022 in a war that began nearly 12 years ago between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and other cities and provinces since September 2014.
Fighting has resumed in several provinces in recent weeks, including Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhalea and Taiz, as the country continues to face one of the world’s worst humanitarian and economic crises.

articles.title: Spanish F-18 shoots down drone over Romania
articles.body:
- A Spanish F-18 on NATO air policing duty shot down a drone over Romania near Galați at 5:01 a.m. Sunday, the fourth such intercept this year.
- The drone entered from Moldova, and its wreckage fell in an unpopulated area between Băleni and Cudalbi with no reported injuries or damage.
A Spanish F-18 fighter jet flying NATO air policing duty shot down a drone that crossed into Romanian airspace early Sunday, marking the fourth drone Romania has shot down this year, the country’s Ministry of National Defence said.
Romanian radar systems detected the aircraft entering national airspace at 4:44 a.m. local time, arriving from neighboring Moldova about 24 km (15 miles) north of Galați. Two Spanish F-18s from the Spanish Air and Space Force, already on alert as a precaution, were dispatched from the 57th Air Base “Mihail Kogălniceanu.” One of the jets established radar contact with the target and received approval to engage. The drone was shot down safely at 5:01 a.m.
“The drone was shot down safely at 05:01 am,” the ministry said.
The ministry did not identify the drone’s origin. A possible impact point for the wreckage was located between the villages of Băleni and Cudalbi in Galați County, in an area the ministry described as unpopulated. The air alert for Galați County was lifted at 5:20 a.m. No injuries or property damage were reported.
Romania’s defense minister, Radu Miruta, confirmed the intercept and credited both the Spanish pilots and the Romanian command center personnel who tracked the incursion, according to Euronews. Miruta said Romania is defending its airspace with the backing of its NATO allies, pointing to the country’s roughly 614-km (382-mile) land border with Ukraine as the reason it sits on what he called the front line of the alliance’s eastern defenses.
The incident is the fourth time Romania has shot down a drone this year. In July, Romanian F-16 pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace, the first time the country had taken that step since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. Earlier this year, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați during an overnight attack on targets across the border in Ukraine, injuring two people.
Romania has scrambled fighter jets in response to airspace incursions multiple times in recent months. Two Spanish F-18s were sent up last Thursday after an airborne object was detected near the river border with Ukraine; that drone spent about 12 minutes over Romanian territory before returning to Ukraine, prompting an SMS alert to residents of Tulcea County. A day later, a separate drone crossed into Romania undetected by radar because it was flying at very low altitude, according to Euronews.
Airspace violations have also been reported elsewhere along NATO’s eastern flank. On Friday, NATO said Italian fighter jets on its air policing mission shot down a drone that had entered Latvian airspace near Balvi. Poland and the Baltic states have reported similar breaches tied to Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Romania’s parliament passed legislation this year authorizing its military to destroy, neutralize or take control of unidentified aircraft that illegally enter its airspace. The bill followed repeated incidents of Russian drones crossing into or crashing on Romanian territory since 2022. Gheorghita Vlad, Romania’s defense chief, had previously called for legal changes to give the military that authority.
The Ministry of National Defence said it is continuing to monitor the situation and is briefing allied structures in real time. The investigation into the drone’s origin and the cause of the incursion remains ongoing.

Russia Builds Up Jet-Powered Drone Strike Hub Near Ukraine. Here’s What Satellite Images Reveal
Russian forces have completed the deployment of 16 launchers for jet-powered attack drones at the Tsymbulova drone base in Russia’s Oryol region, while satellite imagery also shows more than 100 drones stored in the open at the facility.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Strategic Aviation on August 15, the new infrastructure includes 10 launchers designed for Geran-5 drones and six for Geran-4 UAVs. The work was completed over roughly one month.
The facility also contains four launchers for Geran-3 drones and three launchers for the more widely used Geran-2, the Russian designation for Shahed-type attack drones.
Satellite images reviewed by Strategic Aviation show at least 37 Geran-5 and eight Geran-4 jet-powered drones positioned at the site, alongside 56 Geran-2 attack UAVs.
The imagery also indicates that Russia is expanding storage capacity at Tsymbulova. Construction is continuing in the western section of the base, where smaller drone storage buildings are being added alongside larger warehouse facilities.
Russia has additionally installed nearly 100 solar panels across the site. According to Strategic Aviation, they are intended to provide supplementary power for communications equipment, weather stations, and drone guidance systems, increasing the facility’s ability to continue operating during possible power disruptions.
The Tsymbulova drone base is located near the village of Tsymbulova in Russia’s Oryol region, approximately 175–180 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
The expansion comes as Russia increases production of its newer jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said on August 12 that Russian manufacturers are producing approximately 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month, with serial production established at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan.

articles.title: World Archery just reinstated Russia’s flag and anthem, despite its killing more than 760 Ukrainian athletes and coaches since 2022
articles.body:
An international sports body has welcomed Russia back under its flag while Russia keeps killing Ukraine's athletes and civilians. The World Archery Federation has lifted restrictions on Russian athletes, allowing them to compete with their country's identity, including under the Russian flag and anthem, the federation announced.
Russia has killed more than 760 Ukrainian athletes and coaches since the start of the full-scale war, with many others made refugees or losing loved ones to strikes on civilians, and some who took up arms without combat experience. Among them is Ukrainian archer Oleksandr Onyshchuk, a master of sport and European champion, killed fighting the occupiers.
What World Archery decided
The federation acted on an Olympic ruling. Its Executive Board met online on 14 August to review the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) 7 July decision, which confirmed that earlier recommendations restricting Russian athletes no longer applied, then lifted the restrictions on Russian athletes, teams, and officials at its events.
The Russians may now compete fully. They can take part under their national flag and anthem at events including the Archery World Cup and World Championships, and the 2022 restrictions on the Russian flag and anthem were removed, in line with a similar decision on Belarus in May. The federation said participation remains subject to standard eligibility, anti-doping, host-country, and visa requirements, and that it supports the Ukrainian archery community and all affected by the war.
Ukraine calls it sportswashing
For Ukraine, the reinstatement serves Russia's propaganda. Allowing Russian athletes into international competition is a means of sportswashing, spreading disinformation, and legitimizing the aggression against Ukraine before foreign audiences, while presenting Russia as still part of the civilized world.
Ukraine also points to who Russia sends. Ukrainian intelligence has documented Russian athletes who are direct participants in the war, including a lieutenant colonel in Russia's armed forces and a deputy brigade commander who competed internationally, according to Ukraine's Defense Intelligence.
Ukraine's National Olympic Committee called the IOC decision behind the reinstatement premature and unjustified and has appealed it to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The archery ruling arrives as Russia's strikes keep killing Ukrainian civilians and athletes in the war that the returning competitors' flag represents.

A Spanish F-18 fighter jet on a NATO air-policing mission Sunday shot down a drone that had illegally entered Romanian airspace.

articles.title: Ukraine Tests Last Shadow T200 Interceptor Drone, Exceeding Expected Range
articles.body:
Ukraine has tested a new interceptor drone capable of flying more than 120 kilometers (74 miles) as Kyiv seeks cheaper ways to destroy Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) targeting its cities and front lines.
The ‘Last Shadow T200’ reached 122 kilometers (76 miles) during recent combat trials, well beyond the 70-kilometer (43-mile) range originally expected, developer Ukrainska Bavovna told Ukrainian defense news outlet Militarnyi.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The aircraft maintained a stable video link throughout the test, according to the company, potentially expanding the distance over which Ukrainian forces can operate the interceptor.
The T200 is designed to defend cities and operate along the frontline against targets including Shahed and Geran attack drones, Gerbera decoys and Molniya drones, company representatives told Militarnyi.
It has a stated top speed of 300 kilometers (186 miles) per hour, can operate at altitudes of up to 16,400 feet (4,999 meters) and can remain airborne for about an hour at cruising speed.
Ukrainska Bavovna began developing the interceptor last year, and both the airframe and its warhead have been approved for use by Ukraine’s defense ministry.
Anti-spoofing defense
The aircraft is equipped with a movable camera designed to improve target detection.
Its video system can also switch between channels and frequency bands to counter Shtora, a Russian system designed to disrupt or spoof drone video feeds.

Developers are also integrating an automatic terminal-guidance system that would allow an operator to lock onto a target before handing off the final stage of the interception to the drone.
The airframe is produced using 3D printing, but the manufacturer plans to shift to casting within several months to improve durability and allow the aircraft to be reused after multiple landings.
Leader in drone warfare
Ukraine has rapidly expanded itsdomestic drone industry since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, developing everything from long-range strike machines to increasingly sophisticated interceptors.
Interceptor drones now account for around 40% of Ukraine’s kills of Russian Shahed-type drones and other long-range attack UAVs.

Ukrainian authorities allege that the e-commerce company’s warehouses are involved in supplying Russian military needs. Wildberries and the Kremlin have denied that.

In the southern Rostov region, Governor Yury Slyusar reported that three people were killed and one was injured in an attack. He did not specify what facility or area had been targeted.
Vorobyov described the attack on the Moscow region as one of the largest in recent times. Sobyanin said around 600 drones had flown toward Moscow since the evening of August 15, with 201 destroyed over the Moscow region.
The Russian Defense Ministry separately reported that 822 drones had been shot down overnight, without specifying how many drones were not intercepted.
The Ukrainian military has not commented on the strikes.

In Kryviy Rih, an industrial facility was damaged, killing one person and injuring 14 others.

articles.title: On-the-Lam Polish Politician Surfaces in Renegade, Pro-Moscow Moldova Territory
articles.body:
A senior Polish politician on the run from corruption charges and potentially a quarter-century in prison is living in a breakaway, pro-Moscow region of Moldova outside the reach of Interpol and European justice, news agencies in Moldova and Ukraine reported on Tuesday.
Marcin Romanowski, Poland’s former Deputy Minister of Justice, arrived in Tiraspol, a city on the Danube River in the separatist Moldovan region of Transnistria, via Romania, some reports said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A region predominantly populated by ethnic Russians and Ukrainians, Transnistrian “separatists,” supported by Russian regular military troops based there, gained de fact independence from Moldova in a war fought March-July 1992.
The rebel authorities in the statelet claim they run a self-governing republic loyal to Soviet Marxist tenets. Neither the United Nations nor any major state – including Russia – has recognized Transnistria’s autonomy from Moldova.
According to the Polish radio news platform RMF FM, Romanowski, via lawyers, filed a motion in a Warsaw court, dated Aug. 4, to be granted “safe conduct” in which he promised to return to Poland to face justice including potential trial, provided he is guaranteed free movement as the legal process moved forward. The residential address Romanowski submitted in the motion is in Tiraspol, Moldova, the “capital” of Transnistria.
Poland Proposes European Legion With Ukrainian Veterans
It was the first public document specifying Romanowski’s whereabouts in months. He has been out of Poland and seemingly on the run from justice for more than a year and a half, since a European Arrest Warrant was issued for him on Dec. 19, 2024.
On Tuesday, Polish media citing Romanowski’s attorney Bartosz Lewandowski said investigators had rejected Romanowski’s proposition and that he planned to appeal.
RMF FM, citing Przemysław Nowak, spokesperson for the National Prosecutor’s Office, said that Polish law enforcement considers Lewandowski a significant flight risk because of the potentially severe penalty Lewandowski would face if convicted, and that “above all, the suspect’s hiding from law enforcement agencies abroad for over a year and a half.”
Polish prosecutors have accused Romanowski of illegally manipulating public funds including a fund created to help crime victims while in office, and named 11 acts involving the misappropriation of public funds and abuse of power.
Among other official claims, Romanowski is alleged to have embezzled $27 million in state funds, while also attempting to embezzle an additional $15 million.
He also is alleged to have used Justice Fund money ($6.4 million) to purchase Pegasus software for state use. Critics of the software have claimed Pegasus if operated by a European national government would seriously infringe on individual citizen privacy guarantees.
If convicted of all claimed offenses, he could face up to 25 years in prison under Polish law.
Romanowski has denied the allegations and claimed they are politically motivated. According to Polish news reports, once under the arrest warrant, he first took shelter in a Lublin monastery and later traveled to Hungary without the authorities finding him.
In December 2025, Hungary, at the time run by a pro-Moscow/anti-European government, granted protection to Romanowski from prosecution. In May, Polish media reported Romanowski had left Budapest, following the election of a new Hungarian government supporting Europe and rule of law. Unconfirmed reports since then had placed him in the Balkans.
Moldova, a democratic state with EU aspirations, is not obliged to extradite EU citizens wanted by Interpol, but usually cooperates with European law enforcement agencies thanks to bilateral treaties and agreements.
Transnistria is by comparison an island of relative lawlessness without cooperative agreements with practically any state, except Russia. Under normal circumstances an EU citizen wishing to visit Transnistria enters the region via Moldova receiving an automatic 45-day short-term visa. Extension is possible on a by case basis via Transnistrian authorities.
Reports have not fully confirmed when or how Romanowski entered Transnistrian territory. Romanian law enforcement authorities would, as EU officials, be obliged to seek and, if possible, arrest Romanowski, if he had tried to enter Moldova and Transnistria via Romania.
Ukraine shut down border checkpoints between its territory and lands claimed by Transnistria on Feb. 28, 2022.
Since then, Kyiv has banned civilian traffic across the border. And because there are 1,300 Russian troops still based in Transnistria, the Ukrainian Armed Forces (AFU) patrol the frontier on a wartime basis.
Romanowski is a serving member of the Polish parliament for the right-wing, nationalist Law and Justice Party. The party supports what it considers “traditional, conservative values” and opposes tight integration between Poland and European law enforcement structures.
The party historically backed strong Polish support of Ukraine against Russia, but since 2023 has actively agitated against Ukraine, accusing Ukrainian grain producers of unfairly competing with Polish farmers, while also accusing Ukrainian refugees in Poland of being a drain on Polish society. The party is dead set against Ukrainian membership in the EU and NATO.

articles.title: Feature: Aug. 15 -- a day for Japan to deeply reflect on its wartime past
articles.body:
TOKYO, Aug. 16 (Xinhua) -- "The war launched by Japan brought immense suffering to the peoples of Asia and many other countries. I believe Aug. 15 is a day when we must deeply reflect on what Japan did and ask ourselves what we, as Japanese, can do to ensure such events never happen again."
Standing among demonstrators at Tokyo's Awaji Park, Miyazaki, a protester from Osaka, made these remarks to Xinhua on Saturday while attending a rally opposing the notorious Yasukuni Shrine, a symbol of Japan's militarism and wartime aggression.
For much of the world, Aug. 15 marks the anniversary of Japan's unconditional surrender in World War II. However, in Japan, the date usually is known as the "memorial day for the end of the war."
"The fact is that Japan was defeated, yet it labeled that defeat the 'end of the war,'" Miyazaki said.
"Japan launched a reckless war doomed to yield nothing, ultimately leading to disastrous consequences. Calling it the 'end of the war' serves to mask this reality," Miyazaki added.
His words echoed a broader concern voiced by many participants at the rally: that historical reflection is being neglected while symbols associated with Japan's wartime militarism continue to receive official endorsement.
On Saturday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made a monetary offering to the Yasukuni Shrine in her capacity as president of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Before attending her first war memorial ceremony since taking office last year, she also performed a remote act of worship toward the shrine from nearby.
Meanwhile, several cabinet ministers and senior politicians, including Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, LDP Secretary-General Shunichi Suzuki, visited the shrine in person.
By Saturday afternoon, a large number of Japanese citizens gathered at Awaji Park to oppose the Yasukuni Shrine, subsequently staging a protest march. Holding signs reading "Dismantle Yasukuni Shrine," "No to Militarism," "No War State," and "Takaichi Must Resign," the protesters denounced the shrine for reviving the spirit of Japanese militarism.
Miyazaki said Yasukuni Shrine glorifies Japan's wars of aggression by enshrining and honoring soldiers who died fighting in those campaigns, adding that Japanese politicians should absolutely not visit the shrine or offer ritual donations.
Another protester said it was utterly absurd to portray those wartime deaths as "noble sacrifices," noting, "This day (Aug. 15) is a day when Japanese people must engage in deep reflection."
Beyond the shrine itself, many demonstrators expressed alarm over Japan's accelerating military expansion.
Since taking office in October last year, Takaichi's government has pushed ahead with policies toward remilitarization: restructuring the Self-Defense Forces for greater offensive capability, deploying long-range missiles with so-called "enemy base strike capabilities," lifting restrictions on exports of lethal weapons, conducting overseas tests of offensive missiles, and accelerating the development of hypersonic weapons.
Critics argue that these measures represent a significant departure from Japan's long-held principle of "exclusively defense-oriented policy."
Nomura, another participant in the demonstration, said that "Japan is tilting toward war and nationalism -- a trend that absolutely must not be allowed." ■

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down drone in Romania near border with Ukraine
articles.body:
NATO fighter jet shoots down drone in Romania near border with Ukraine
Romania's defense ministry said Sunday a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone that had entered its airspace near the border with two of its neighboring countries Ukraine and Moldova.
The ministry said in a statement the drone had entered from Moldova and was intercepted by an Spanish F-18 jet deployed on NATO duties early Sunday morning. Debris fell in an unpopulated area near the border with Ukraine, the ministry added.
The interception is the latest in a series of similar recurring incidents involving drones straying into Ukraine's neighboring countries borders, which authorities have blamed on electronic interference as part of the war with Russia. In some cases, the drones are Ukrainian and are "hijacked" by Russian forces.
Authorities have reported finding drone fragments on Romanian soil several times since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube River, which lie just across the border. Last week, Ukraine denied targeting Bulgaria after a drone entered the country's airspace on Saturday and exploded close to an international gas pipeline shortly after crossing the border from Romania.
Last month, Romania shot down a drone for the first time since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, after it entered the country's airspace about 60 miles from Bucharest.
In June, Latvia's military said two NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the country's airspace. Ukrainian drones have previously crashed in all three Baltic states, which all share borders with Russia, with officials blaming the inadvertent incursion on Russian electronic warfare.

articles.title: Red Sea Mocha port in Yemen closed following over 25 Houthi missile attacks
articles.body:
Yemen's Mocha port has suspended commercial and maritime operations after being hit by more than 25 missiles in Houthi attacks over recent days, the port's director said on Saturday.
The attacks killed seven people and caused an estimated $16 million in losses, the director told a news conference.
Mocha is a Red Sea port near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a strategic chokepoint connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a key route for international shipping.
Forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government control the port. It has a smaller cargo capacity than Yemen's main ports of Aden and Hodeidah.
Yemen's government said on Friday the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at Mocha that day, killing at least four civilians and targeting civilian, economic, and maritime facilities.
Houthis claim to target weapons, warships
The Houthis said they targeted a military build-up of weapons and warships belonging to Saudi-backed forces in Mocha.
The escalation comes amid heightened regional tensions from the US war on Iran and has raised concerns about a return to large-scale conflict in Yemen.
Major fighting in Yemen had largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but efforts to reach a lasting political settlement have stalled.

articles.title: The first anti-AI protester to be jailed has a message for OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta: ‘Regain your humanity’
articles.body:
An activist who blocked the entrance to one of the world’s biggest AI companies is believed to have become the first person jailed for protesting against artificial intelligence as supporters dub her the “Rosa Parks of AI risk”.
Wynd Kaufman, 69, surrendered herself on Friday to authorities in San Francisco. She was found guilty by a jury for her role in an action last year that saw members of the group StopAI chain and lock the front doors of OpenAI’s headquarters in protest against the pursuit of artificial superintelligence.
The retired teacher from Berkeley, California, refused to move from a sit-in protest in February 2025 and pleaded not guilty to multiple misdemeanor charges. She was convicted in June of interfering with a business, trespassing with intent to interfere with a business, unlawful assembly and refusal to disburse a riot. On Friday, sheriff’s officers handcuffed her as fellow campaigners sang to the tune of the Battle Hymn of the Republic (Glory, Glory Hallelujah): “Rise up, rise up and join us/Do not let the tech bros destroy us.”
“It’s absolutely frightening and appalling that these CEOs and AI experts know the dangers and they are pursuing it anyway,” Kaufmyn said before she was imprisoned. “That to me is unconscionable and reprehensible.”
She said she was willing to go to jail not because she was a martyr but because it was an “issue of sounding the alarm, challenging the system and hopefully trying to get the message out”.
Brooke Jenkins, the San Francisco district attorney, said the guilty verdict sent “a resounding message rejecting the notion that protesters can endanger public safety as a means to an end”.
As Kaufmyn was led out from the court, her supporters called out: “Stop AI” and: “Free Wynd” as the sheriff’s officer yelled: “Clear the court” and the judge admonished the protesters.
Dwight Ost, 73, one of two dozen other StopAI activists at the courthouse, called Kaufmyn “a brave and courageous woman”.
“There’s an existential threat that I believe in,” he said. “They can’t control it, and even the so-called experts don’t know what it’s about.”
Kaufmyn had argued that the protest was a necessity and that she believed she was allowed to act to prevent a greater harm from happening. Since the lobby sit-in last year, some of the biggest AI labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have reported their models escaping the confinements of experiments.
This week, the US senator Bernie Sanders demanded tech leaders pause AI development, citing fears that, in the wrong hands, it might “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”.
Meanwhile, more than a thousand researchers at frontier AI labs this summer signed a letter warning of “a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems”.
Frontier AI labs are locked in a race to create more capable AI models as the companies target IPOs that are forecast to reach valuations in the trillions of dollars. At the same time, Washington is competing with Beijing for supremacy in the fast-developing technology, creating a disincentive for tougher safety regulation.
“The jury rejected [Kayfmyn’s] necessity defence, but as the first person to go to jail over this, Wynd Kaufmyn could go down in history as the Rosa Parks of AI risk,” said David Kreuger, a University of Montreal AI safety expert who has warned AI “may literally lead to human extinction, in the same way that humans have caused many other species to go extinct”. Parks was a Black woman who refused to give up her bus seat for a white passenger in contravention of racist segregation laws in 1950s Alabama, a catalyzing incident for the US civil rights movement of the ensuing decade.
Kaufmyn spoke on the eve of her imprisonment from her shingled house in Berkeley, which is festooned with Mexican tiles and pro-Gaza signs. She played down the Parks parallel, pointing out her short sentence, but said the comparison had also crossed the campaign group’s mind, given that she is thought to be the first AI protester jailed.
She said that when she was found guilty, she was “hit with a wave of grief” because she realised her peers “just didn’t get” the danger she believes is posed by the race to superintelligence. But she was beginning to feel “vindicated” as more prominent figures like Sanders were speaking out. She is now braced for the prison experience of an orange jump suit, “horrible food, dirt [and] you can’t sleep”. She has been previously jailed for short periods related to her decades of political activism over causes including Nicaragua, nuclear disarmament, western Sahara and Palestine.
Her message to the chief executives of OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta, which also reported a security incident with its model, was “regain your humanity”. Kaufman said her target audience was ordinary people “and the message being: stop the progress of this technology. Let’s get a global ban on the race to superintelligence.”
Professor Stuart Russell, a leading AI professor at the University of California at Berkeley and president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI, gave evidence in Kaufmyn’s defence. He claimed OpenAI’s activities “pose an unacceptable risk”, alleging it had deployed AI systems with inadequate safeguards. He said that further development of these systems “must be conditioned on rigorous guarantees of safety, which are currently unavailable”.
Russell said: “Wynd stood up for her beliefs and is being punished.” He said her beliefs seemed reasonable but “what is unreasonable is allowing a process to continue whereby private entities knowingly create a substantial extinction risk for private gain”.
StopAI has been roiled by its own controversies. Last November, its co-founder, Sam Kirchner, 27, went missing after an internal bust-up over whether or not to use violent tactics. He is said to have told colleagues the “non-violence ship has sailed”, raising concerns he might take violent action against OpenAI employees. StopAI aims to pursue non-violent direct action.
OpenAI was approached for comment.

The two Koreas are still technically at war after their 1950-53 war ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

articles.title: US Representative McCaul warns warns of China's belligerence toward Taiwan
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — US Rep. Michael McCaul, chair emeritus of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, warned that China's increasingly belligerent threats toward Taiwan pose a direct challenge to the global balance of power during his third visit to Taiwan, per VOA.
McCaul, a Republican from Texas, visited Taiwan from Aug. 2-7, meeting with President Lai Ching-te (賴清德), Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍). He also delivered a speech at the annual Ketagalan Forum, where he reiterated US support under the Taiwan Relations Act.
"At a time when the stakes couldn't be higher, I was proud to visit Taiwan for the third time to reaffirm the United States' unwavering support," McCaul said in a statement. "The increasing belligerence of the Chinese Communist Party poses a direct threat — not only to Taiwan, but to the entire global balance of power," per a press release.
McCaul said he has consistently supported Taiwan, including efforts to advance the 2024 Supplemental Appropriations Act and strengthen US-Taiwan economic relations. He also highlighted his support for closer security cooperation among the US, Australia, and the United Kingdom. In recognition of his support for Taiwan, Lai awarded McCaul the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Brilliant Star.
McCaul previously announced that he would not seek reelection after his current term in Congress expires.
During his visit, McCaul also met with opposition leaders, including Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), and legislators from opposition parties. Discussions covered Taiwan's recently passed defense budget, the importance of drones, and US-Taiwan cooperation on drone production.
Before leaving Taiwan, McCaul also met with officials from the National Security Council and Ministry of National Defense to exchange views on strengthening Taiwan's defenses against China's coercive actions in the region. He also visited US drone company Shield AI and the Industrial Technology Research Institute, where he learned about Taiwan's drone industry and ITRI's certification work.
ITRI is the first institution outside the US authorized to certify that drones do not contain components from China, per VOA.
McCaul, a member of the House of Representatives Taiwan Caucus, first visited Taiwan in April 2023 as chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. He returned in May 2024 to attend Lai's inauguration.
China conducted military exercises involving aircraft and naval forces around Taiwan during both of those visits and imposed sanctions on McCaul. During his latest visit, McCaul said China's coercive actions had only strengthened his commitment to supporting a free and peaceful Taiwan.

The spokesperson said Tehran had yet to respond to an invitation to review details of its operations.
An Iranian military official on Sunday accused Qatari officials of repeatedly delaying the investigation and preventing the pilots' return to Iran.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff, said an Iranian Air Force expert and fact-finding team had been waiting for months to enter Qatar, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
"Due to persistent delays by Qatari authorities, the return of our brave pilots to their homeland remains impossible," he was quoted as saying.
Baqerzadeh also said Kuwait was similarly withholding information about the fate of four Iranians held in Kuwait. In May, Iran said the four were affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards and had been on a maritime patrol before entering Kuwaiti territorial waters because of a navigation disruption. Kuwait has said the four were suspected of planning hostile actions against the country.
Iran's army said last month it had retrieved the body of pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during an attack on Qatar's Al Udeid Air Base in early March.
Iranian authorities previously declared the other pilots missing but did not allege they had been captured in Qatar.
Al Udeid is the largest US military base in the Middle East and has been used by US Central Command (CENTCOM) in the six-month war against Iran.
The US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, which triggered retaliatory Iranian attacks across the region.
Diplomatic efforts led to an April ceasefire that ended nearly 40 days of fighting, followed by the signing of a framework for peace talks in June that later collapsed.
The two countries have since traded fire sporadically, with fighting mainly centred in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Qatar, which took part in mediation efforts to end the fighting, came under fire after the truce broke down, reporting attacks on its territory and at least one Qatari tanker transiting the strait.
(Agencies and TNA staff)

articles.title: ‘No Room for Mistakes’: What Next for Protestors Demanding Fedorov’s Reinstatement?
articles.body:
On Sunday Aug. 16, a significant rally in support of Mykhailo Fedorov, along with a demand for the continuation of reforms at the Ministry of Defense, is due to take place in central Kyiv. However, the focus of recent protests is already shifting beyond these boundaries, with many of the banners and placards no longer mentioning Fedorov.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the Aug. 14 rally, broader grievances against the authorities came to the fore – corruption, non-transparent decision-making, not listening to the people, and even the cutting down of 100-year-old oak trees in one of Kyiv’s districts for the benefit of developers, which has stirred anger among local residents.
                                                                                                                                                                         
One of the main slogans of last week’s large march, which gathered more than 10,000 people, was “Listening to the people – that’s powerful,” where the word “powerful,” which President Volodymyr Zelensky had previously used extensively, was employed as a form of trolling.
Zelensky Confirms Flamingo Missile Strikes Deep in Russian Territory
However, the future of the rallies is now very much in question.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Many commentators believe that, despite the uncertainty surrounding Fedorov himself (he said that negotiations with representatives of the authorities are still ongoing), President Zelensky is unlikely to be considering the option of returning him to the position of head of the Ministry of Defense.
Why?
First, General Yevhenii Khmara has already been introduced to key players and foreign partners as acting minister of defense; and second, the president cannot risk showing to the hierarchy that he is willing to give in to the street on everything.
                                                                                                                                                                         
The situation is made even more uncertain by Fedorov himself. He has not come out to the people on Maidan – that would have meant his transition into active politics – and he has indicated a lack of desire to criticize President Zelensky until the end of the war.
In a conversation with prominent civic activist Serhiy Sternenko, Fedorov said: “I will not lead the protest, because it will be perceived as a political move. And our task is to win the war.”
According to several journalists and political strategists, this is a mistake.
Ukrainian journalist Maryna Danyliuk-Yermolayeva stated. “Yes, Yushchenko’s emergence among the wider masses as a talented economist turned him into an icon of the national democrats. Yulia Tymoshenko’s appearances among the people cemented her for a long time as the people’s darling, the princess of Ukrainian politics. The same ride on a road grader by Petro Poroshenko at the dawn of the Revolution of Dignity instantly propelled the former minister in Azarov’s government to the top of the ratings… Fedorov said in an interview with The New York Times that he would not be in opposition until the end of the war. But it is worth saying that after that there will be new heroes. And they will certainly know how to go out into the streets and meet with people.”
The future of the protests therefore look ambiguous.
The largest rally, “The Last Attempt to Reach the President,” is due to take place on Sunday Aug. 16. On Tuesday Aug. 18, during parliament’s plenary week, lawmakers will vote for the new head of the Ministry of Defense.
Will the rallies continue if it becomes clear that Fedorov will definitely not return to his former ministerial post?
And if they do continue, how long can they last?
For now, this question remains open. All the more so because the main grievance of part of society toward Zelensky is not so much about Fedorov as it is about the systemic problems that forced Zelensky to dismiss the defense minister – even knowing that this would cause dissatisfaction.

articles.title: NATO fighter shoots down suspected Russian drone that illegally entered Romanian airspace
articles.body:
An F-18 fighter on a NATO air policing mission shot down a drone that illegally breached Romanian national airspace, the fourth unmanned aircraft shot down over the country this year, Romania's Defense Ministry said on Sunday.
A spokesperson for NATO's military headquarters, US Army Colonel Martin O'Donnell, said the alliance is constantly on watch and prepared to defend itself from any threat.
"Additional details regarding Sunday’s incident remain under investigation, but the drone appears to be Russian," he said.
NATO member Romania shares a 614 km. land border with Ukraine and has reported repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over the past four years, as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and energy routes.
Romania's defense ministry did not specify the origin of the drone, saying it was detected by radar as it entered the country from neighboring Moldova, 24 km. north of the southeastern Romanian city of Galati.
The F-18 jet, part of a Spanish NATO contingent deployed in Romania, "made radar contact with the target and received permission to engage", the ministry said in a statement, adding that the drone was shot down safely at 5:01 a.m. (0201 GMT).
The ministry said that fragments from the destroyed drone appeared to have fallen in an uninhabited area between two villages.
Russia reportedly sends drones to Romania to breach NATO airspace
In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down three Russian drones breaching national airspace for the first time after dozens of such incursions since the start of Russia's war in Ukraine.
In May, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment block in Galati during an overnight attack on neighboring Ukraine, injuring two people.

articles.title: The 1991 treaty that still haunts the Kremlin
articles.body:
As Russia wages war on Ukraine, denying its own history of aggression against its neighbours, a little-known treaty signed 35 years ago is quietly getting in the way of the Kremlin's narrative.
In July 1991, five months before the Soviet Union formally dissolved, Russia signed a treaty with Lithuania in which it recognised something Moscow has spent the past two decades trying to erase from the record: that the Soviet Union illegally annexed Lithuania in 1940, and that Lithuania's independence, declared in 1990, was legitimate.
That document is still in force. Russia has never torn it up. And that, say Lithuanian officials and legal experts, makes it an awkward loose end for a Kremlin that now insists the Baltic states were never really occupied at all.
Under President Vladimir Putin, Russian state doctrine has increasingly leaned on the claim that the Baltic states joined the USSR voluntarily, and that talk of "occupation" is Western-backed revisionism.
That framing underpins not only Moscow's rhetoric towards Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia but also, in a broader sense, the ideological justification for its invasion of Ukraine – the idea that the borders and independence of post-Soviet states are negotiable, or fictional.
The 1991 treaty directly contradicts that. Dainius Žalimas, a Lithuanian MEP who has studied the treaty closely, argues that its first article, which has no expiry date, remains one of Lithuania's strongest legal cards: it commits both countries to recognising each other as sovereign states with an inalienable right to independence, and bars either from meddling in each other's internal affairs as well as using or threatening force against the other.
"All of this essentially refutes every claim made by current official Russian propaganda, and undermines the very foundations of the ideology of 'rashism'. That ideology, which underpins both the aggression against Ukraine and the denial of Baltic statehood, recognises neither the occupation of Lithuania nor the continuity of the Lithuanian state, among much else," said Žalimas.
"I think the treaty is very important. We talk about the wavering authority of international law, but it gives Lithuania a solid line of international legal defence, and shows that Russia, for very brief periods in its history, can be different," he added.
For example, Lithuania can continue to demand compensation from Russia for the damage caused by occupation, even though few believe this will ever happen in practice.
"Just as the treaty of July 12, 1920 formed the basis for all subsequent treaties with the Soviet Union, the same applies here – dozens of Lithuanian-Russian agreements rest on the July 29, 1991 treaty. So the treaty still holds, as long as they haven't broken it," explained Česlovas Vytautas Stankevičius, former deputy chairman of the Supreme Council and head of the negotiating delegation with Russia, highlighting why the treaty still carries weight to this day.
How it came about
The path to the treaty began in secrecy. In May 1990, Vytautas Landsbergis, then chairman of Lithuania's Supreme Council (the country's parliament in the final Soviet years), held a clandestine meeting with Boris Yeltsin, his Russian counterpart, in an empty Moscow school classroom. The two men barely knew each other personally, and the meeting was arranged through informal contacts.
Two months later, leaders of the three Baltic states and Russia met in the Latvian town of Jūrmala and agreed to pursue bilateral treaties – partly as a way of applying pressure on Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader, who was still trying to hold the union together.
That effort was not merely symbolic. The USSR spent 1990 and 1991 trying to force Lithuania, as well as other republics, back into line, including a 75-day economic blockade after its declaration of independence.
At the time, it was unclear whether it was better to negotiate with the Soviet leadership or with Russia, which in June 1990 had issued its own declaration of state sovereignty. As a result, negotiations proceeded with both the Soviet authorities and with Yeltsin's Russia, which proved to be a great decision since once the Soviet Union collapsed, Russia became its legal successor.
For Lithuania, negotiating and signing the treaty meant securing the backing of the largest Soviet republic for its independence – a powerful argument against the Soviet Union. Meanwhile, Russia's leadership was competing during with the central Soviet authorities for control.
"The goals of the two states coincided," summarized Stankevičius, who was appointed head of Lithuania's negotiating delegation.
Having concluded treaties with Latvia and Estonia, Russia wanted to sign a similar document with Lithuania.
But Lithuania's treaty took longer to conclude, largely because Vilnius pushed for tougher language than Moscow wanted to accept.
The sticking points
Negotiators clashed over three issues in particular.
The first was citizenship. Lithuania wanted to prevent members of the Soviet military and security apparatus – as well as their families – from automatically qualifying for Lithuanian citizenship, while also avoiding a settlement that would let ethnic Russians resident in the country claim dual nationality.
A compromise formula eventually restricted citizenship rights to those with ties to Russia who had lived and worked in Lithuania since before November 1989.
The second was how to characterise the movement of people under Soviet rule – specifically, how to avoid a formula that would have put Lithuanians deported to Russia by Stalin's regime in the same legal category as Russians who had been resettled into Lithuania as part of Soviet colonisation policy.
The two sides eventually agreed on the neutral term "relocating persons" to cover both groups without equating them politically.
Finally, the thorniest question – whether Russia would accept responsibility for the 1940 annexation – was resolved not by the negotiating teams but by Landsbergis and Yeltsin personally.
"The Russian negotiators didn't want to accept responsibility for crimes committed by the Bolsheviks – all those acts of violence and coercion against neighbouring states. They didn't want the responsibility. Their position was that the Russian Federation, in restoring its own statehood, would not take on responsibility for the crimes of the communist regime," Stankevičius told LRT.lt.
Meanwhile, Landsbergis's own public position at the time was that responsibility lay with the USSR rather than Russia specifically.
So, the compromise text kept a reference to the 1940 annexation while dropping Lithuania's request to invoke an earlier, 1920 peace treaty in which Soviet Russia had renounced all claims to Lithuanian territory, making it's later Soviet occupation – illegal.
The irony
That compromise proved more significant than either side may have anticipated. When the Soviet Union collapsed months later, Russia inherited its rights and obligations as successor state – including, Lithuanian officials argue, responsibility for the consequences of the 1940 annexation that Russia itself had just agreed to acknowledge. And so, it was obliged to remedy the damage, withdraw its troops, and so on.
Three and a half decades on, the treaty's core value lies precisely in the fact that it is Moscow's own signature on a document that says the opposite of what the Kremlin now claims.

articles.title: Ukraine Wipes Out 75 Russian Drones Over Sumy, Including Rare $100,000 Knyaz Veschyi Oleg
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Wipes Out 75 Russian Drones Over Sumy, Including Rare $100,000 Knyaz Veschyi Oleg
Ukrainian air-defense drone operators have destroyed 75 Russian aerial targets over Sumy region since the beginning of August, including 53 Molniya-2 strike drones and a rare Knyaz Veschyi Oleg reconnaissance UAV valued at around $100,000.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade “Magura” reported on August 15 that its Sky Wars unit had intercepted 53 Molniya-2 drones, six ZALA Lancet loitering munitions, six FPV drones, three ZALA reconnaissance UAVs, three Gerbera drones, two drones identified as “Bombers,” one Knyaz Veschyi Oleg and one Mavic quadcopter.
Molniya-2s accounted for more than two-thirds of the total. The fixed-wing Russian FPV drone is designed as a relatively inexpensive platform for tactical strikes and reconnaissance.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to the President of Ukraine on defense technology development, estimated its cost at about $1,600, putting the value of the 53 destroyed aircraft at roughly $84,800.
The six Lancets represent a significantly more expensive part of the losses. Developed by ZALA Aero, the Lancet family consists of loitering munitions used to locate and strike battlefield targets.
Beskrestnov estimated the newer X-52 at around $40,000 and the larger X-51 at about $68,000. Since the brigade did not specify the variants, the six destroyed Lancets could be worth approximately $240,000 to $408,000.
Among the rarest targets was the Knyaz Veschyi Oleg, a Russian tactical reconnaissance UAV developed by the Ushkuynik research and production center.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence lists it as having a 2.8-meter wingspan, endurance of up to 3.5 hours, an operational radius of around 45 kilometers and a maximum speed of 130 km/h. Ukrainian military units have previously valued the drone at approximately $100,000.
Sky Wars also destroyed three Gerbera drones. The Russian UAV is built largely from inexpensive materials and is commonly used as a decoy resembling Shahed-type attack drones, although reconnaissance and armed variants also exist.
Ukrainian estimates have placed its production cost at around $10,000 per aircraft, giving the three destroyed Gerberas an estimated value of about $30,000.
The brigade did not specify the models of the three ZALA reconnaissance UAVs, six FPVs, two “Bombers,” or the Mavic, making their value difficult to determine reliably.
Based only on the 53 Molniya-2s, six Lancets, three Gerberas and the Knyaz Veschyi Oleg, the 63 identifiable drones had an estimated combined value of approximately $454,800 to $622,800. The real total for all 75 destroyed aircraft would therefore be higher.
Ukraine has also been pushing interceptor drones to greater altitudes. On August 2, border guards using a STING FPV interceptor destroyed a Russian ZALA Z-20 reconnaissance UAV at 6,858 meters over Chernihiv region, setting what Ukrainian authorities described as a world record for drone-on-drone interception.
