articles.title: Should Iran negotiate with U.S. again?
articles.body:
In recent days, the Trump administration, after accepting undeniable defeats and bearing very heavy military costs, especially human casualties, has again leaned towards negotiations and agreements and, as in the past, is trying to convince Iran to negotiate by applying pressure and intimidation.
Iran believes that the goal of negotiations is to reach a common understanding acceptable to the negotiators and for the parties to adhere to the implementation of their commitments. In response to the invitation for negotiations from the United States, Iran accepted Pakistan's mediation, and detailed negotiations were held with good intentions and strong will at the level of the Speaker of the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Iran's parliament) and the Vice President of the United States. This decision showed that Iran is determined to use diplomacy to secure the legitimate interests of the Iranian people, oppose war and tension, and end the oppressive sanctions.
The result of these negotiations led to the signing of a 14-point memorandum of understanding by the presidents of the two countries, with the assumption that Trump would respect his signature and adhere to the implementation of the memorandum's provisions. However, in practice, this did not happen, and the hostile moves of the United States with numerous attacks on southern Iran and the continuation of the naval blockade showed that the White House is not loyal to diplomacy and negotiations, but is also using this soft resource as a prelude to war and aggression.
Although the Islamic Republic of Iran welcomes diplomacy, it does not like the formula of negotiation for the sake of negotiation. Negotiations are valuable when they are aimed at achieving results and the parties are committed to implementing their commitments. At the current stage, there is no reason to conduct talks again, because in the previous negotiation, a memorandum of understanding was signed at the presidential level and is available. If for the United States, the invalidation of the president's signature does not matter, in Iran, the president's signature is valid and the provisions of the memorandum of understanding that was signed must be implemented to stop the war and resolve the remaining disputes.
Conducting negotiations to understand the demands and intentions of the other side was a logical and intelligent move, but today, not only Tehran but also many politicians around the world are skeptical about the seriousness of the American side in implementing the understandings and do not recommend repeating the failed negotiation. Of course, intermediary countries such as Pakistan and Qatar are active and convey messages, but conveying messages does not mean negotiating, and in the current situation, there is no desire and will on the Iranian side to negotiate with the United States. In fact, when the United States has failed in the test of negotiations and implementing the understandings, how can we talk about holding talks again?
The experience of negotiating several times with the United States shows that this country, due to its reliance on military, economic, and security power, only thinks about securing its own and Israel interests and wants immediate concessions from the other side and in return, only makes empty promises. The Islamic Republic of Iran, while being powerful, does not welcome war and tension, and at the same time does not accept the approach of negotiation for the sake of negotiation.

articles.title: Trump’s midterm malaise: endless war and high prices could spell doom for Republicans in November
articles.body:
He was always one step ahead. Donald Trump won the US presidency as a wildly unlikely outsider in 2016 and staged an astonishing comeback to win it again in 2024. Even his foes grudgingly called him a political savant with an intuition for exploiting grievances that left so-called experts floundering.
But now they are asking if the dark genius has lost his touch. Trump is trapped in the quagmire of an unpopular war, obsessing over monuments in Washington and looking for a new spokesperson after his White House press secretary quit. If the 80-year-old was deliberately trying to sabotage his Republican party in November’s midterm elections, it is not clear what he would do differently.
“He’s always had a reptilian political instinct for public opinion that has served him well,” said Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster. “You’re not seeing that much any more. You’re not seeing his ability to read the room. He seems tone-deaf on issues like the cost of living, the war, and the optics of gilding everything in sight and enshittifying Washington and he doesn’t care.”
Trump campaigned on promises to lower prices and keep the US out of foreign entanglements and forever wars. The opposite has happened. Voters say they are suffering a cost of living crisis, exacerbated by Trump’s sweeping tariffs. Buying food to eat at home has become 33% more expensive in US cities since the beginning of 2019, according to government figures.
Gas prices are at a record high for this time of year, in part thanks to the US war in Iran, which drags on with no end in sight. While Trump claims to have destroyed Iran’s military capabilities, it emerged this week that he was forced to hide in a catering truck and secretly swap planes after a Nato summit in Turkey because of a possible Iranian assassination plot.
The administration’s entanglement has metastasised into a gruelling, daily haemorrhage of resources, currently costing the taxpayer an estimated $1bn a day. Critics argue the administration has strengthened Iran’s resolve and provided it with global leverage, specifically over the strait of Hormuz. They see it as betrayal of the noninterventionist posture that fuelled Trump’s rise to power and attracted a generation of disaffected voters.
Kurt Bardella, a political commentator and former congressional aide, said: “What we’re watching right now is the complete unraveling of everything that Donald Trump, Maga and Republicans said they were about. They were against endless conflicts in the Middle East and they started a conflict in the Middle East without an exit strategy. They were supposed to be about no more spending American dollars abroad; we’re spending a billion dollars a day on this war without an end.”
Yet the president appears to have other, more aesthetic concerns. Since returning to power last year, the longtime property developer has invested much time and energy in construction projects across Washington, including a White House ballroom and helipad, a triumphal arch and an ill-fated makeover of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.
Bardella added: “As he continues this misadventure in the Middle East that has resulted in the cost of living going up, and continues to pour resources into putting his name on shit and building ballrooms and monuments to himself, the American people are going: what the fuck? That’s the only realistic reaction you could have when you objectively look at the circumstances.”
Trump’s second term has been defined by thinking big – Greenland, Venezuela, Iran – and thinking small. The board he appointed to the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts added his name to the complex, only for a judge to order that it be removed; this week the board voted to add “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J Trump” beneath the main sign.
According to Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, written by New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, the president has been seen with a tube of super glue trying to stick golden decorations to the marble fireplace in the Oval Office.
Haberman estimates that Trump now devotes 70% of his mental space to renovation projects and “monuments to self”. She told Axios’s Behind the Curtain video series that she and Swan visited Trump in the Oval Office in March. “You would think that on the 17th day of the war that he would have maps of the Middle East or maps of troop deployments – who knows,” she said. “He picks up these pictures, and [they’re] of maple trees, and he says: ‘I am choosing maple trees for the White House. I am good at picking trees.’ I’m paraphrasing here, but that is pretty much what he said.”
The president’s preoccupation with whether columns for his ballroom are more evocative of Athens or Rome, and with other efforts to preserve his legacy in marble, come as little surprise to Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill and longtime Trump critic.
She said: “Donald Trump has been an egomaniac, a narcissist his entire life. Even in the private sector he has slapped his name on buildings and a multitude of failed branding businesses from Trump steaks to Trump airline to Trump University to Trump water to Trump wine. Why is anyone surprised that he would take that same type of narcissism and bring it over to his role in his second-term as president when he’s spending other people’s money to do it?
“The problem has been that the Republican party has enabled him to get away with this and to their own detriment, which is why more and more people in his inner circle are concerned about how this is going to impact the midterms and control of Congress.”
Indeed, Republicans are said to be quietly panicking about Trump costing them the House of Representatives and putting even the Senate in jeopardy. A national Quinnipiac University Poll released late last month showed his job approval rating dropping to an all-time low of 32%, with 58% disapproval. It found six in 10 Americans oppose the US military action in Iran.
Past presidents such as George W Bush in 2006 and Barack Obama in 2010 have faced challenging midterms but worked with their parties in an effort to at least stem the losses. Rick Wilson, co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, said: “In both those cases their efforts were not successful, but it’s nightmarish to think what that would have been if Barack Obama had been saying, ‘I’m going to build a basketball arena at the White House,’ or George Bush had said, ‘I’m gonna build a golf course.’
“Instead you’ve got a very different visual from this White House and that visual is 'we don’t care about anything else except for the ballroom and the arch and all the throw-away ephemera that he wants to focus on. It’s a terrible political look and it’s quite dangerous for the party because they have nothing to run on right now.”
The sense of malaise deepened this week when Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person ever to serve as White House press secretary, announced that she will be stepping down at the end of the month. The official explanation was that the 28-year-old wants to spend more time with her young family but the timing was unfortunate for an administration struggling to spin its way out of one crisis after another.
For a president whose entire self-image is built on winning, the realisation that he is facing electoral defeat at home and humiliation abroad could be cause for an existential crisis. Sykes observed that, while Trump’s historical literacy is notoriously thin, he has begun to obsess over the ghosts of presidencies ruined by foreign blunders.
“It’s awfully interesting that in the Maggie Haberman book he’s comparing himself to Napoleon and Alexander the Great and Caesar but his deepest fear right now is that he’s going to be Herbert Hoover or Jimmy Carter,” he said.
Trump’s cloud does have a golden lining, however. He made an estimated $2.2bn during the first year of his second term thanks to cryptocurrency holdings, foreign interests and his Truth Social business.
Sykes added: “He hasn’t lowered the cost of living, he hasn’t made America more respected, he hasn’t won the war but he has succeeded in making himself a billionaire many times over by abusing his office.”

articles.title: NATO fighter jets shoot down drone over Romania near Moldova border
articles.body:
Two Spanish F-18s deployed in Romania for a NATO mission on Sunday intercepted and destroyed an unidentified drone near the Moldovan border, Romania’s defence minister Radu Miruta confirmed.
Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets, which were already on alert as a precaution, received authorisation to intervene at 04:44 on Sunday morning. The drone was sighted 24 kilometres north of the town of Galati.
The drone, whose origin has not been confirmed by the Romanian authorities, was intercepted and destroyed between the towns of Baleni and Cudalbi, in the south-east of the country, in an area close to the border with Moldova.
The defence minister congratulated both the Spanish pilots and the Romanian military personnel in charge of the command centre. In his message, Miruta stressed that Romania "is defending its airspace" and that it has the backing of its allies, which he described as a tangible security guarantee based on vigilance, rapid response and solidarity among the countries of the Alliance.
The minister emphasised that Romania is on the front line of the European Union's defence, a position he attributes to the roughly 614 kilometres of land border the country shares with Ukraine.
The incident also comes after another night of exchanges of attacks between Russia and Ukraine. Russian bombardments triggered large fires in Kyiv, with at least two people injured, while Moscow claimed it had been targeted by more than 600 drones launched by Kyiv, leaving three people wounded on Russian territory.
A string of incidents on the eastern flank
This latest incident adds to a long list of incursions recorded in recent weeks in Romanian airspace.
Last Thursday, two Spanish F-18s had already taken off from the Mihail Kogălniceanu base after an airborne object was detected near the river border with Ukraine, a drone that spent around 12 minutes in Romanian territory before returning to Ukraine, forcing the authorities to send an SMS alert to residents of Tulcea county.
A day later, while a drone crashed in Romania after crossing the country's airspace undetected by radar because it was flying at very low altitude, tensions were also mounting in the Baltic, where allied fighter jets shot down another drone over Latvian territory.
At the start of the month, another unidentified device exploded in Bulgarian airspace, near the border with Romania, after entering from Romanian territory.
The most serious precedent dates back to 29 May, when a Russian drone struck a residential block in Galati, sparked a fire and injured two people, in what the Atlantic Alliance at the time described as an irresponsible escalation by Russia.
The NATO secretary-general, Mark Rutte, reiterated at the time that the organisation is ready to defend every inch of allied territory against this type of threat.

Russian Spending Abroad Hits 11-Year Record at $23.3 Billion in Six Months
Russians spent an estimated $23.3 billion on foreign travel in the first half of 2026, the highest amount for the period in 11 years, as a stronger ruble earlier in the year and disruptions affecting domestic and international travel routes boosted spending abroad.

The figure comes from Russia’s Central Bank data on imports of services under the “travel” category, which largely reflects spending by Russian residents while abroad, The Moscow Times reported on August 15. The total was 14% higher than during the same period in 2025 and approached the $23.9 billion recorded in the first half of 2014.
Russia’s Central Bank estimated that overall services imports increased 16% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, reaching $87 billion. The regulator attributed part of the increase to higher average costs of foreign travel packages.
Travel disruptions in the Middle East contributed to those higher prices. Fighting involving Iran forced some Russian tourists traveling to South and Southeast Asia to switch from connecting flights through the region to more expensive direct services.
Others postponed previously planned trips and faced higher prices when rebooking, according to the Central Bank’s balance-of-payments commentary cited by The Moscow Times.
A senior executive at a major Russian tour operator estimated that postponing trips during disruptions in the Persian Gulf in April increased their cost by around 10% to 20%. Direct flights to destinations such as Thailand and the Maldives can also cost roughly one-third more than connecting services, the executive said.
Foreign travel increased in volume as well. According to estimates from the Association of Tour Operators of Russia cited by The Moscow Times, Russians made approximately 9.5 million tourist trips abroad between January and June, an 8.7% increase from the same period last year.
Vietnam, China and Egypt accounted for nearly all of that growth, collectively adding about 1.3 million trips. China has also become more important as a destination and transit hub following the introduction of visa-free travel for Russians in September 2025.
The Central Bank noted that a growing share of Russian travelers heading to other Asian destinations also passed through Chinese airports.
In 2025, Russians spent an estimated $49.7 billion on foreign travel. The historical peak remains 2014, when annual spending abroad reached $50.4 billion.
The rise in foreign travel spending comes alongside broader Russian demand for options abroad. Demand for overseas property rose 20% in the first half of 2026, with analysts linking the increase partly to concerns over a possible new wave of military mobilization.

articles.title: Morocco arrests more than 100 people near Ceuta border
articles.body:
Moroccan police arrested at least 111 people attempting to reach the Spanish territory of Ceuta on Saturday after calls circulated on social media for another mass border crossing. Authorities in Morocco and Spain deployed security forces around the border following the arrival of tens of thousands of people in Ceuta two weeks earlier.
A Moroccan Interior Ministry source told Reuters that 109 of those detained were migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two were Moroccan citizens.
The arrests took place in and around Fnideq, a coastal town about three kilometres from the Ceuta border.
Groups travelled through hills outside Fnideq in an apparent effort to avoid security checkpoints. Spanish news agency EFE reported that Moroccan police used tear gas to disperse people gathered in the area.
Reuters later saw hundreds of Moroccan officers returning from the hills, including police in riot equipment and plain-clothes personnel.
The official arrest figure differed from figures reported by Moroccan media. Local outlet Le360 put the number at 294, including 46 Moroccans. Authorities had not confirmed that higher figure.
Morocco increased security after online messages called for a mass crossing on 15 August. The government said earlier in the week that it was monitoring posts of unknown origin and warned that organisers and participants faced prosecution.
Moroccan forces deployed police, military personnel, naval vessels and drones near the border. Authorities also established checkpoints and prevented some groups from taking trains and buses towards northern Morocco.
Spain increased its presence on the other side of the border. More than 1,600 police officers were deployed in Ceuta after Madrid sent over 500 additional officers from mainland Spain, Reuters reported. Spain also installed a maritime barrier following the previous influx.
The security operation followed a mass arrival on 30 July, when more than 72,000 people entered Ceuta.
At least 96 people died during the crossing, according to Reuters.
Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Thursday that about 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta. He said people who entered without authorisation would not be transferred to mainland Spain or granted legal status except in cases involving vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would face return to Morocco.
The July arrivals also led to disputes between European Union states. Italy introduced border controls on arrivals from Spain, citing migration concerns. Spain responded with controls of its own after asking Rome to withdraw the measure.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Saturday that Italy had feared another large arrival in Ceuta.
“We're not waging any kind of ‘battle’ against Spain,” Tajani said. “We're simply carefully controlling arrivals.”
Ceuta lies on the North African coast and shares a land border with Morocco. Spain administers the territory, while Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty over the enclave.

We’re hurting. We’ve lost our most successful manager in decades, plus his talismanic captain. A-listers have departed and we’ve been humiliated in the transfer market, for the second summer running. Yes, a reset was needed, but we weren’t expecting it to be like this. At least, in Matthias Jaissle, we have a hungry, passionate young manager whose intensity will be welcomed. He certainly looks up for the fight and, despite our outgoings, the German has some exciting talent to work with. According to CEO David Hopkinson, this is “Newcastle United 2.0”. We guess we’ll know what that means in a few months’ time.
Key players/weak links Lewis Miley is “one of our own” and, with Tonali gone, can fulfil his potential. We’ll also be expecting improvements between the posts, with Lukas Hornicek and Ewen Jaouen competing for the keeper’s jersey. And if Yoane Wissa and Anthony Elanga can replicate their World Cup form, we might have a strike force on our hands. The weak links? Joe Willock, who contributed very little to the cause last season and, sadly, Sven Botman, whose form has never recovered from his anterior cruciate ligament injury in 2024.
We still need to sign … A replacement for Bruno Guimarães, leaders on and off the field, high-grade cover at both full-back positions, a centre-half … so not too much to ask … Benfica’s versatile full-back Amar Dedić and Milan’s centre-half Fikayo Tomori would certainly be a good start. Crucially, we need to blend more experience into our youthful side, but any deals will have to be done in stealth mode, given Liverpool’s recent behaviour …
Our cult hero is … Big Dan Burn. A giant of a man, with a heart to match.
If we could sign two players from our past … Alan Shearer for his leadership and goals, and of course, the much-loved, and much-missed, Kevin Keegan. Both knew what it meant to wear the black-and-white shirt.
We will finish 10th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Liverpool; 4. Chelsea. Bottom three: 18. Ipswich; 19. Coventry; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Álvaro Arbeloa.
- 
  David and Richard Holmes
Nottingham Forest
If nothing else, it can’t be as chaotic as last season. We survived fairly comfortably in the end – thanks Vítor! – then sacked him in favour of Glasner, with the rationale being that the Austrian has won silverware. So the target this time isn’t only a decent league finish, but also something in the cabinet.
Key players/weak links The key, like last season, will be Morgan Gibbs-White: the talisman, the on-pitch leader, and the guy who makes things happen for the Reds. After being overlooked for Tommy T’s England squad, he will be keen to continue to show his worth.
We still need to sign … Getting Ousmane Diomande feels important; Murillo and Milenkovic make a great pair but we were still vulnerable in defence last season, and the new guy should balance with the attributes of the established duo. For all that we have loads of wingers, we do desperately need a reliable striker: we can’t continue to rely on a 35-year-old with a chronic knee problem.
Our cult hero is … Fans of other clubs love to take a swipe at our owner, and Reds supporters are frequently quick to jump to his defence. For all the controversies, I genuinely think Marinakis has been great for Forest and for English football: ruthlessly ambitious, aware that decision-making carries risk as well as reward, and unwilling to shrink in the face of so-called “big clubs” or the authorities. He has made some high-profile mistakes but does not shy away from making big calls (sorry Vítor!). And, of course, as Palace fans are aware (along with most of Greece), the Big Guy will also stand up for what he thinks is right and proper, and doesn’t care what other people think.
If we could sign two players from our past … Stan Collymore and Des Walker: pace, power, brilliance.
We will finish 12th. Top four 1. Chelsea; 2. Arsenal; 3. Liverpool; 4. Man United. Bottom three 18. Crystal Palace; 19. Coventry; 20. Hull. First manager sacked De Zerbi.
- 
  Rich Ferraro, 1865: The Nottingham Forest Podcast
Sunderland
I’m optimistic – but definitely cautiously optimistic. Last season completely exceeded our expectations and finishing seventh with Europa League football on the horizon was incredible. However, Europe changes things. The biggest challenge will be managing the extra games without losing the spark that made us so enjoyable to watch. I’d be very happy with a comfortable mid-table finish and a decent European run. Consolidating ourselves in the league has to be the priority.
Key players/weak links Xhaka is still absolutely pivotal – he brings so much leadership and control – while Le Fée is probably the player I most enjoy watching. I’m also really excited to see what Talbi does this year. He was managed really well last season without too much pressure being put on him, but this feels like his season to really kick on. I don’t think there’s an obvious individual weak link; the concern is whether we have enough depth to compete on multiple fronts.
We still need to sign … I’d still like another attacking option, ideally someone who can play on the right and offer genuine end product. Geny Catamo is an interesting link, but I know the club won’t move unless the figures line up. More than anything, I want quality depth. We could play a ridiculous number of games this season, so we need options rather than simply another big name.
Our cult hero is … Wilson Isidor without question. His “football is life, Sunderland is life” clip probably summed it up perfectly. He gets the club and we genuinely love him. Add in the personality, the goals and his ability to do something brilliant or completely chaotic, and he feels destined to go viral several times this season.
If we could sign two players from our past … Kevin Phillips is the obvious first choice. Put peak Phillips alongside Brobbey and you’ve got a ruthless finisher playing off someone who can hold the ball up and occupy defenders. My second would be Amad. He’d give us quality, creativity and unpredictability out wide, and after how loved he was during his loan spell, bringing him back would feel like a proper homecoming. Put Amad on the wing with Phillips and Brobbey through the middle and I’d be getting dangerously carried away very quickly.
We will finish 12th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Liverpool; 4. Manchester United. Bottom three: 18. Fulham; 19. Coventry; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Sergej Jakirovic.
- 
  Eleanor McCabe @eleanor_amc for @WiseMenSayPod, wisemensay.co.uk
Tottenham
Nothing screams more “Tottenham Hotspur” than stating we’re going to have an outstanding season having finished 17th twice in succession and narrowly avoided relegation. We probably should have gone down. Somehow West Ham managed to be a little bit more rubbish than a team that could barely win home games. Roberto De Zerbi and Enic’s personality change (spending money on end products) is why I’m flirting with the idea of a top-five finish. Absolute greed on my part, but it’s fun to believe. Top eight would be grand.
Key players/weak links Still work to do, but the backline has been rebooted and Micky van de Ven has signed a new contract. In midfield, with Tonali and Fernandes (two of the best mids available to sign) and with Kudus and Deki to return, we finally have depth and quality and strength. The aim will be to galvanise and rejuvenate our home form and regain that confidence and swagger. The key is De Zerbi. His appointment has changed everything. As for youngsters, Luca Williams-Barnett has all the potential to be something special.
We still need to sign … We’ll need plenty done over the next few windows, but ideally, we could do with a winger (we’ve been chasing Savinho for what feels forever) plus a No 10 and a forward. Maddison getting injured again is a concern. We need more than just Solanke up top, with Richy likely to leave.
Our cult hero is … Djed Spence for his World Cup heroics – but we are selling him to Inter. So it has to be the Spurs social media team, the togetherness vibe is the feelgood cleansing we need.
If we could sign two players from our past … It’s a cheat code, but let’s add Harry Kane to the frontline and Gareth Bale to the wing (or any position he wants).
We will finish 17th/1st. Top four: 1. Tottenham; 2. Manchester City; 3. Liverpool; 4. Manchester United. Bottom three: 18. Nottingham Forest; 19. Newcastle; 20. Aston Villa. First manager sacked Mikel Arteta.
- 
  Spooky The Fighting Cock podcast; @DearMrLevy; Filthy Shambles podcast on Spotify

articles.title: Myanmar leader to visit Russia for talks with Putin
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
16 August 2026•Update: 16 August 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold talks with his Myanmar counterpart Min Aung Hlaing at the Kremlin on Tuesday, Aug. 18, during the Myanmar leader’s official visit to Russia, the Kremlin said Sunday.
 
The two leaders will discuss prospects for expanding Russian-Myanmar cooperation in various areas, as well as current international and regional issues, it said in a statement.
 
Several bilateral documents are also expected to be signed during the visit, it added.
 
Putin and Min Aung Hlaing have held talks on several occasions in recent years, including at the Kremlin in March 2025.
 
Russia and Myanmar maintain close political and defense ties, with Moscow also involved in energy and infrastructure projects in the Southeast Asian country.
 
Min Aung Hlaing visited Russia three times last year — in March for talks with Putin, in May to attend a military parade marking the 80th anniversary of victory in World War II and in September to take part in the World Atomic Week forum.
 
Putin has never visited Myanmar.
